# Preview, check, publish (/data-scientist/communicate/preview-check-publish)



## Preview, check, publish [#preview-check-publish]

The code enforces the order. You cannot skip a step.

<Flow
  caption="The order is enforced: a preview that was not checked is never published"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;Preview&#x22;, text: &#x22;The kit checks the workflow, the read-only identity and Dash Server's profile, then creates the preview&#x22;, code: &#x22;print(\&#x22;Preview:\&#x22;, dash_server.url + preview_path)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Check&#x22;, text: &#x22;Open the preview and compare the figures with the SQL&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Publish&#x22;, text: &#x22;confirm refuses unless figures_checked is True and the preview is healthy&#x22;, code: &#x22;dashboard_draft.confirm(dash_server, figures_checked=True)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
]"
/>

## Before you preview: Dash Server [#before-you-preview-dash-server]

The notebook calls `nb.dash_tools()`, which starts Dash Server if it is stopped. Dash Server is a kit add-on. The add-on is installed with `exakit marketplace dash-server`. The [add-ons page](/kit/tools/add-ons) explains how add-ons work.

```python
dash_server = nb.dash_tools()                     # starts Dash Server if it is stopped
preview_path = dashboard_draft.preview(dash_server)
print("Preview:", dash_server.url + preview_path)
```

### Preview [#preview]

`preview` checks four things before it creates anything:

* that the workflow is the one the dashboard was made in
* that the read-only identity is validated
* that Dash Server's profile is the kit's read-only user on the kit's database
* that the dashboard's name is not already taken by a dashboard that belongs to another dataset, or that has no readable lineage

Then it creates the preview, confirms that the built copy holds the approved SQL and lineage files unchanged, and runs a health check. A preview that fails the health check is marked unhealthy, and the kit will not publish it.

### Check [#check]

Open the preview and compare the figures with the SQL. Use the page described on [What a reader sees](/data-scientist/communicate/what-a-reader-sees). The chart's grouped Other figure is one to check against the query. Only a person can make this check. The notebook never does it for you.

### Publish [#publish]

`FIGURES_CHECKED` is `False` in `03_share`. Set it to `True` after the check, and run the cell. In code:

```python
live_path = dashboard_draft.confirm(dash_server, figures_checked=True)
```

`confirm` refuses unless `figures_checked=True` and the preview is healthy. It promotes that exact revision, starts the app if it is not mounted, and checks the live address. If the live check fails, the error says to roll back in Dash Server.

In automated runs the check is never set, so nothing is published without a person.

## The workflow log [#the-workflow-log]

Each preview and each publish adds a line to the workflow log, with the query's digest, the descriptor version and the revision number. The kinds are listed on [The workflow log](/data-scientist/monitor/the-workflow-log).

Back to [Communicate and deploy](/data-scientist/communicate). Next: [What a reader sees](/data-scientist/communicate/what-a-reader-sees).


# The training hand-off (/data-scientist/communicate/training-hand-off)



## The training hand-off [#the-training-hand-off]

The training hand-off is the ML Engineer's file. It is one JSON file with the feature view, the target, the split and the training SQL. The Data Scientist notebooks do not write it. The ML Engineer's notebook writes one if none exists.

```python
path = nb.write_handoff(conn, ds)     # writes the file and returns its path
```

`nb.write_handoff(conn, ds)` writes the file to `~/.exasol-starter-kit/handoffs/<id>-v<n>.json`, where `<n>` is the descriptor's version. `nb.read_handoff` reads it back. The file names a table, columns, SQL and digests. It never names a host, a user or a password.

## The split [#the-split]

Two rules decide how the rows are split for training:

* **A date in the column map gives a time split.** This is the default. The oldest rows train the model and the newest rows test it.
* **No date means no time split.** The kit refuses a time split that the data cannot support, and names the fix. A dataset with no date, such as `fraud_transactions`, needs a split named on purpose: `nb.write_handoff(conn, ds, split="random")`.

The kit does not choose a random split for you. `split="random"` is a reproducible hash of each row's role columns, so the same rows always give the same split.

## When the hand-off goes stale [#when-the-hand-off-goes-stale]

A hand-off that no longer matches the column map or the data is refused. The check and the fix are on [A training hand-off that went stale](/data-scientist/monitor/stale-hand-off).

Back to [Communicate and deploy](/data-scientist/communicate). Next: [Deploying a model](/data-scientist/communicate/deploying-a-model).


# Troubleshooting (/data-scientist/communicate/troubleshooting)



Each entry quotes the message or describes the step that stops.

<Accordions type="multiple">
  <Accordion title="Dash Server is stopped or missing">
    The notebook installs and starts it when you call `nb.dash_tools()` or `nb.addon_ready("dash-server")`. To do it yourself, run `exakit marketplace dash-server`, then `exakit start dash-server`, then `exakit status` to confirm. See [Add-ons](/kit/tools/add-ons).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Resume the workflow before previewing or promoting">
    The dashboard belongs to the workflow it was made in. Run `nb.continue_workflow("share")` in this notebook, or resume the workflow with `nb.workflow(resume="wf-...")`, and try again.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="The read-only identity is not validated, or the profile is wrong">
    The preview needs the kit's read-only user to be validated. Run `exakit mcp-doctor` to check it. When the message says the profile must validate as the read-only user, run `exakit mcp-setup`, then restart Dash Server.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="The dashboard name already exists without readable lineage">
    The error reads "choose another APP_NAME". The name is taken by a dashboard the kit did not make, or one made for another dataset. Choose another `APP_NAME`. The kit never overwrites a dashboard that belongs to a different dataset.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="The preview is unhealthy">
    The health check failed, so the kit will not publish it. The error reads "Dash Server preview is unhealthy". Open the Dash Server log with `exakit logs dash-server`, fix the cause, and run the preview again.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="confirm asks you to open the healthy preview">
    `confirm` was called without `figures_checked=True`, or the preview is not healthy. Check the figures against the SQL, then confirm again. See [Preview, check, publish](/data-scientist/communicate/preview-check-publish).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="The live dashboard failed its health check">
    The error reads "use app_rollback in Dash Server". The published revision is not healthy. Roll back there, then check the preview again before you publish another revision.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="The hand-off is refused as stale">
    The training hand-off no longer matches the column map or the data. Read the line the kit prints, then write the hand-off again with `nb.write_handoff(conn, ds)`. See [A training hand-off that went stale](/data-scientist/monitor/stale-hand-off).
  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

Back to [Communicate and deploy](/data-scientist/communicate).


# What a reader sees (/data-scientist/communicate/what-a-reader-sees)



## What a reader sees [#what-a-reader-sees]

The dashboard is a view of the reviewed SQL result. It is not a new calculation over the table. Its page says so.

* **Filters.** Categories, a Show setting (10 by default), Sort by, and Chart layout (horizontal or vertical bars). Top N applies after the filters. **Reset filters** clears them.
* **Category comparison.** A bar chart of the values in the current selection.
* **Composition.** A share-of-total chart. The kit draws it only when you pass `measure="count"`, because a total of a measure that is not a count has no meaning. With more than eight rows shown, the note says smaller categories are grouped as Other.
* **Behind the charts.** The same filtered rows as a table, sortable, with **Export CSV**.

## Check the figures against the SQL [#check-the-figures-against-the-sql]

When you check a preview, compare three things with the query on [Build the dashboard query](/data-scientist/communicate/dashboard-query):

1. The category names in the table match the values in the query's first column.
2. The counts match the counts the query returns. `nb.show_sql()` prints the last query the notebook ran.
3. The composition chart's Other group equals the sum of the categories it groups.

```python
nb.show_sql()   # the SQL the last query ran
```

Back to [Preview, check, publish](/data-scientist/communicate/preview-check-publish). Next: [The hand-off bundle](/data-scientist/communicate/hand-off-bundle).


# Approve the column map (/data-scientist/explore/approve-the-column-map)



Approval makes a draft column map count. The kit checks it, saves it as a new version, and publishes it for the schema's semantic model. Use the guided card or the notebook. The same checks run either way.

<Flow
  caption="What happens when you approve a column map"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;You approve&#x22;, text: &#x22;Approve column map in the card, or call approve in a cell&#x22;, code: &#x22;role_review.approve({...}, {...})&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The kit checks&#x22;, text: &#x22;roles, slots, the table unchanged, the leakage check&#x22;, code: &#x22;exakit describe <id> --approve&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Semantic model rebuilt&#x22;, text: &#x22;SEM_<SCHEMA> in Exasol Semantic Views&#x22;, tone: &#x22;db&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/explore/semantic-views&#x22; },
]"
/>

## What approval checks and writes [#what-approval-checks-and-writes]

* Every column has a role, and no column sits in two slots.
* The table has not changed since the kit profiled it.
* The data is checked again. A column that gives the target away is reported. The column stays in the map and is left out of the model. See [Columns that give the answer away](/data-scientist/prepare/leakage).
* The next **version** is written to the kit's store on this computer, under `~/.exasol-starter-kit/descriptors/`.
* The roles are published in Exasol Semantic Views. The schema's model is rebuilt: its time, category and flag columns become dimensions, and its measures become facts with `total_` and `average_` metrics. A sensitive column is never exposed. If publishing fails, the approval still stands, and the message says why.
* The active workflow's log gets one line.

When the kit has no Semantic Views in the database, it installs the semantic-views add-on first, the same as `exakit marketplace semantic-views`.

## Worked example: amazon_sales [#worked-example-amazon_sales]

The worked example uses `amazon_sales`, the sample orders table: `AMAZON.ORDER_LINES`. The kit ships an approved column map for it. The map is the one you would get if you approved the proposal without change.

The shipped map gives these slots:

| Slot       | Column          | Why                          |
| ---------- | --------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `key`      | `ORDER_LINE_ID` | one row per order line       |
| `time`     | `ORDER_DATE`    | when the order was placed    |
| `text`     | none            | the table has no free text   |
| `target`   | `CANCELLED`     | the outcome a model predicts |
| `category` | `CATEGORY`      | the groups to compare        |
| `entity`   | `SHIP_STATE`    | where the order went         |

Three things in the map are worth reading before you approve it:

* **Check these first.** The card lists the columns the kit was least sure about, first. `SHIP_CITY` and `SHIP_STATE` are both drafted at low confidence. The kit's evidence for `SHIP_STATE` is 47 distinct values. The card shows that evidence beside it.
* **Personal data.** `SHIP_POSTAL_CODE` is marked sensitive. It is never charted, grouped or sent to a model.
* **The answer.** `STATUS` is a category with 13 values, and it gives the answer away: a cancelled order has a cancelled status. The approval warns about it, and the model leaves it out. The [leakage check](/data-scientist/prepare/leakage) explains how.

Approve in the card with **Approve column map**, or in the notebook:

```python
role_review = nb.review_roles(connection, chosen_data)
role_review.approve({"SHIP_CITY": "identifier"}, {"target": "CANCELLED"})   # for example: a role you change, and a slot you set
dataset = role_review.dataset()
nb.show_roles(dataset)
```

The first argument holds the roles you change. The second holds the slots. With nothing to change, the saved approval stands.

On a table directly, with no review:

```python
draft = nb.describe("AMAZON.ORDER_LINES")
draft.set(SHIP_CITY="identifier")      # for example: a role you change
draft.slot(target="CANCELLED")         # the outcome to predict: you choose it
dataset = draft.approve()
```

After the approval, the cell that follows it runs the leakage check. The printed line for a column that gives the answer away has this form:

```text
- STATUS gives CANCELLED away: CANCELLED is 1 whenever STATUS is '...'. It was probably written after the outcome - leave it out of any model.
```

The text in the quotes depends on the data, so the cell prints the value it found.

## Versions [#versions]

Every approval is a new version. Nothing is overwritten.

```python
nb.column_map_versions(dataset.id)     # every saved version, oldest first
nb.current_version(dataset.id)         # the approved one
```

Approving an older version's roles again brings it back as the newest version. In the card, **Version history** lists each version with what changed, and **Restore** saves an older version's choices as a new one.

To change the roles later, open the quickstart, change them and approve again. The other notebooks follow the newest approval when you run their first cell again.

Back to [Explore and understand](/data-scientist/explore). Previous: [The column map](/data-scientist/explore/column-map). Next: [Semantic views](/data-scientist/explore/semantic-views).


# The column map (/data-scientist/explore/column-map)



A **column map** says what each column of a table is for. Its technical name is the **descriptor**, the word you see in code and in some file names. Every later query is built from the column map, so no notebook types your column names. A notebook asks for "the time column" or "the target", and the column map gives the name.

## The column map and approval [#the-column-map-and-approval]

The kit drafts the column map from the table itself. The draft is a proposal. You approve it before any other step reads it. Approval checks the map and saves it as a new version. The steps are on [Approve the column map](/data-scientist/explore/approve-the-column-map).

### Roles: what a column is [#roles-what-a-column-is]

The kit profiles the table in SQL and gives every column one of eight roles. It also records the evidence that chose the role.

| Role         | Meaning                       |
| ------------ | ----------------------------- |
| `key`        | One value per row             |
| `time`       | A date or timestamp           |
| `measure`    | A number to add up or average |
| `category`   | A few repeated values         |
| `flag`       | Yes or no                     |
| `text`       | Free text                     |
| `identifier` | Names or codes                |
| `other`      | None of the above             |

A **confidence** says how close the evidence is to the line the rule draws. It is not a probability that the business meaning is right. Low-confidence columns come first in the review. For `amazon_sales`, the card lists `SHIP_CITY` and `SHIP_STATE` first, both drafted at low confidence. The card shows the evidence beside each column. For `SHIP_STATE` that evidence is 47 distinct values.

### Slots: which column each step uses [#slots-which-column-each-step-uses]

A **slot** names the one column a step reads.

| Slot       | Used for                      |
| ---------- | ----------------------------- |
| `key`      | Counting rows without repeats |
| `time`     | Anything over time            |
| `text`     | The text steps                |
| `target`   | The outcome to predict        |
| `category` | The groups to compare         |
| `entity`   | Who or what a row is about    |

A column fills one slot at most. A slot can be empty when no column fits. An empty slot says why.

The kit's shipped datasets have these slots:

| Dataset            | `key`           | `time`       | `text` | `target`     | `category`         | `entity`     |
| ------------------ | --------------- | ------------ | ------ | ------------ | ------------------ | ------------ |
| Amazon sales       | `ORDER_LINE_ID` | `ORDER_DATE` | none   | `CANCELLED`  | `CATEGORY`         | `SHIP_STATE` |
| Fraud transactions | `ROW_ID`        | none         | none   | `FRAUDULENT` | `TRANSACTION_TYPE` | `LOCATION`   |

In code, two slots keep their older names: `dataset.col("date")` is the `time` slot, and `dataset.col("label")` is the `target`.

### The target is yours to choose [#the-target-is-yours-to-choose]

The kit never chooses the **target**, the outcome a model predicts. You do. It must be a column of 0 and 1, or true and false. The card reads the target's values and says how common the outcome is. The rule is in `target_verdict` in `notebook/package/exakit_guide/screens/understand.py`:

* A target that holds values other than 0 and 1 cannot be predicted. The card says the kit can't count or predict it.
* A target that is 1 in under 1% of rows is too rare to learn from reliably.
* A target that is 1 in under 5% of rows is rare but workable, as in fraud.
* Anything else is a good balance to learn from.

For `amazon_sales`, `CANCELLED` is 1 in 14.2% of rows (18,332 of 128,975, measured). By that rule it sits in the balanced band.

Two 0/1 columns can answer different questions. Pick the one that is the outcome you want to predict.

### Draft and approved [#draft-and-approved]

A column map starts as a **draft**. A draft can be wrong, and nothing downstream uses it. Explore, Ask and Share open only an **approved** dataset. A step given a draft raises `DescriptorNotApproved`, and the message says how to approve it.

A model never approves roles. The kit never chooses the target. You approve.

## Draft a column map for a table [#draft-a-column-map-for-a-table]

To see the kit's proposal for one table, without the review card:

```python
draft = nb.describe("AMAZON.ORDER_LINES")
```

```bash
exakit describe AMAZON.ORDER_LINES
```

A draft is not approved, and no later step reads it. Read the roles and slots, then approve them as described on [Approve the column map](/data-scientist/explore/approve-the-column-map).

Back to [Explore and understand](/data-scientist/explore). Next: [Approve the column map](/data-scientist/explore/approve-the-column-map).


# Compare groups and trends (/data-scientist/explore/compare-groups)



Comparing groups answers the first question about most tables: how many rows are in each group, and does the outcome differ between groups? Comparing over time answers whether the counts or the outcome rate move. The kit runs both on the approved dataset. It shows the SQL before each result, and writes a plain-language note under it, so a result is not read without its meaning.

## Compare groups and trends [#compare-groups-and-trends]

`01_explore` runs two kinds of query on the approved dataset. Each query shows its SQL before its result, and a plain-language note under it.

* **Compare groups.** The ten largest entities, with the row count of each category and the percentage where the target is 1.
* **Over time.** Rows per period, and the percentage where the target is 1. The period is chosen by the span of the data: a day when the span is up to 62 days, a month up to three years, otherwise a year.

```python
rows = nb.sql(connection, f"""
SELECT {dataset.col("category")} AS GROUP_, COUNT(*) AS N
FROM {dataset.fact_table}
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY N DESC""")
nb.show_sql()                              # the SQL the last query ran
```

`nb.note_groups` and `nb.note_trend` write the notes under each result. A note says what one row of the result is, in the data's own words, and what the overall figure is. It names the highest and lowest groups. It says which groups have too few rows to trust their percentage. It also says that a difference between groups is not a cause.

Groups with fewer than 30 rows are not compared, because one row moves their percentage a lot.

A step that needs a column the dataset does not have skips and says why. The Compare step needs a category, an entity and a target. The Over time step needs a time and a target.

## The worked example [#the-worked-example]

The worked example uses `amazon_sales`. The dataset README records 128,975 order lines and 14.2% cancelled. Measured on the database, the table holds 128,975 rows, and 18,332 of them have `CANCELLED = 1`, which is 14.2%.

The time span runs from 31 March to 29 June 2022, which is 90 days, so the over-time step groups by month. The first query above returns one row for each category, with its row count.

Three of the category counts were measured through the semantic model, which counts the prepared view of the table (128,969 rows, not the table's 128,975). They are the order lines in each category: Set 50,281, kurta 49,874 and Western Dress 15,500. See [Semantic views](/data-scientist/explore/semantic-views). The repository does not record the output of the notebook's group query itself. To see it, run the cell in `01_explore`.

A difference between groups is a pattern in the data, not a cause. Check a difference against the notes before you act on it.

Back to [Explore and understand](/data-scientist/explore). Previous: [Linked tables](/data-scientist/explore/linked-tables). Next: [Ask questions in plain language](/data-scientist/explore/questions).


# Is my data sent anywhere? (/data-scientist/explore/data-privacy)



Not by default. The database and the notebooks run on this computer. A step sends data to an AI model only when you set up a model and turn the step on. The steps below say what each one sends.

## Is my data sent anywhere? [#is-my-data-sent-anywhere]

Not by default. The database and the notebooks run on this computer.

* With no model set up, every step runs on this computer. The rules drafter for Ask sends nothing.
* With a model set up, Ask sends the approved column map and your question. It never sends rows.
* The themes step sends a sample of texts, and it is off until you turn it on. It is in `01_explore`: set `USE_AI_THEMES = True` in the first cell, with a model set up. Your model then sorts the newest texts where the target is 1 and where it is 0 into themes. It makes two model calls.
* A table from a live external source asks before any sampled rows go to a model.
* The semantic model's AI proposal receives names, types, grains, column notes and a category's most frequent values. It never receives a row, and never a sensitive column. See [Semantic views](/data-scientist/explore/semantic-views#the-ai-proposes-the-fields).

Sensitive columns are never sent to a model. See [The column map](/data-scientist/explore/column-map) for how the kit marks them.

Back to [Explore and understand](/data-scientist/explore). Previous: [Ask questions in plain language](/data-scientist/explore/questions). Next: [When it goes wrong](/data-scientist/explore/troubleshooting).


# Explore and understand (/data-scientist/explore)



Before you compute anything from data, you need to know what each column means. Is `CUSTOMER_ID` a name or a count? Is `ORDER_DATE` the day of the order or the day of delivery? Which column is the outcome you want to predict? In this stage the kit proposes an answer for every column, and you confirm it. Once you approve the answers, every later step reads them, and so does every AI client that asks the database.

<Flow
  caption="What happens when you approve a column map"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;You approve&#x22;, text: &#x22;Approve the column map in the card, or call approve in a cell&#x22;, code: &#x22;role_review.approve({...}, {...})&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The kit checks&#x22;, text: &#x22;Every column has a role, no column sits in two slots, the table has not changed&#x22;, code: &#x22;exakit describe AMAZON.ORDER_LINES --approve&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;A new version is saved&#x22;, text: &#x22;The next version of the column map, under the kit's own folder on this computer&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The semantic model is rebuilt&#x22;, text: &#x22;The schema's model in Exasol Semantic Views, the database's semantic layer&#x22;, tone: &#x22;db&#x22;, href: &#x22;/kit/data/semantic-views&#x22; },
]"
/>

## The flow [#the-flow]

Explore has three parts. Each one reads the approved column map.

1. **The column map.** The kit proposes a role for every column. You approve the roles and the slots.
2. **The semantic model.** Approving publishes the schema's model in Exasol Semantic Views. A semantic model is a named layer over the tables. It says which columns are groups, which are numbers to add up, and how tables link. You can also build one model that spans several sources.
3. **Explore and ask.** You compare groups and trends, and ask questions. A question you ask runs only after you approve its SQL.

## Where you do it [#where-you-do-it]

| Guided view                                                                                    | Notebook code                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Terminal                                                                                                                                                               |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Understand** in `00_quickstart`: the **Column map** card and the **Semantic views** section. | `00_quickstart`, *Approve the column map*: `nb.review_roles`, `role_review.approve(...)`, `nb.show_roles`, `nb.leakage_check`, `nb.column_map_versions`, `nb.data_map`. *Semantic views*: `nb.semantic_model`, `nb.semantic_sql`, `nb.refresh_semantic`, `nb.semantic_models`. | `exakit describe SCHEMA.TABLE` to draft. `--approve` to approve. `--show`, `--versions`. `--schema` for links. `--model`, `--refresh`, `--models` for semantic models. |
| **Working on** and **Compare groups and see trends** in `01_explore`.                          | `01_explore`: `nb.sql` with `nb.show_sql()`, `nb.note_groups`, `nb.note_trend`.                                                                                                                                                                                                | None. These run in the notebook.                                                                                                                                       |
| **Ask** in `02_ask_your_data`.                                                                 | `02_ask_your_data`: `nb.example_questions`, `nb.draft_question`, `nb.ask`, `proposal.edit(...)`, `proposal.approve()`, `proposal.run()`.                                                                                                                                       | None.                                                                                                                                                                  |

The notebooks keep their choices in their first cell. `DATASET = None` follows the dataset you approved last.

## What you have at the end [#what-you-have-at-the-end]

An approved column map, saved as a version, and a published semantic model that AI clients can read. You have also seen how the tables link, and you have compared groups and asked questions with queries you approved.

Next: [Prepare](/data-scientist/prepare).

# Linked tables (/data-scientist/explore/linked-tables)



Many datasets are several tables. Orders link to customers, and orders link to products. A **schema map** shows how the tables of one schema fit together. It lists every table with its rows and its key, and every link between tables, with the evidence for it. You check the map here, so that the semantic model and the AI clients can follow the links correctly.

## The schema map: how tables link [#the-schema-map-how-tables-link]

```python
schema_map = nb.describe_schema(connection, dataset)   # the tables and the links, as found now
schema_map
```

```bash
exakit describe --schema AMAZON
```

A link is a column whose values are all in another table's key. The kit finds two kinds:

* a foreign key the database declares, or
* a column that names another table's key, such as `O_CUSTKEY` and `C_CUSTKEY`, or `CUSTOMER_ID` and `CUSTOMERS.ID`, whose values are all in that key. At most 0.1% of its values may be missing. A name alone never makes a link.

The kit's search is in `describe_schema` in `notebook/package/exakit_nb/schema_map.py`. Each link it finds shows the evidence beside it.

## Correct the map [#correct-the-map]

Correct the map when the search misses a link or finds a wrong one:

```python
schema_map.link("ORDERS.CUSTOMER_REF", "CUSTOMERS.ID")   # a link the search missed
schema_map.unlink("ORDERS.O_CLERK")                      # a link that is wrong
schema_map.approve(connection)                           # the links become relationships in the schema's model
```

```bash
exakit describe --schema TPCH --approve --link ORDERS.O_CUSTKEY=CUSTOMER.C_CUSTKEY
exakit describe --schema TPCH --approve --unlink ORDERS.O_CLERK
```

<Flow
  caption="What happens when you approve a schema map"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;The kit finds the links&#x22;, text: &#x22;Every many-to-one link, with the evidence for it&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.describe_schema(connection, dataset)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;You correct the map&#x22;, text: &#x22;Add a link the search missed, or remove a wrong one&#x22;, code: &#x22;schema_map.link(...)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;You approve it&#x22;, text: &#x22;The next version of the schema map is saved&#x22;, code: &#x22;schema_map.approve(connection)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The links become relationships&#x22;, text: &#x22;In the schema's semantic model, for AI clients&#x22;, tone: &#x22;db&#x22;, href: &#x22;/kit/data/semantic-views&#x22; },
]"
/>

Approving the schema map writes its next version. It rebuilds the schema's semantic model with the links as relationships, so AI clients can follow them. The schema's own tables are never changed.

## Where the links go next [#where-the-links-go-next]

* The links become relationships in the semantic model. See [Semantic views](/data-scientist/explore/semantic-views).
* The joined view brings linked columns into one wide view of one table. It is built in the Prepare stage: see [Linked tables and the joined view](/data-scientist/prepare/linked-tables-view).

Back to [Explore and understand](/data-scientist/explore). Previous: [Semantic views](/data-scientist/explore/semantic-views). Next: [Compare groups and trends](/data-scientist/explore/compare-groups).


# Ask questions in plain language (/data-scientist/explore/questions)



You can ask a question in English. The kit drafts one read-only SQL query. You read it, approve it, and only then does it run. Nothing runs against your data before you approve the exact text, and the query runs as a read-only user.

## Questions in plain language [#questions-in-plain-language]

Ask a question in English. The kit drafts one read-only SQL query. You read it, approve it, and only then does it run.

<Flow
  caption="What happens to a question"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;You ask&#x22;, text: &#x22;A question in plain language, about an approved dataset&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.draft_question(connection, dataset, QUESTION)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;A query is drafted&#x22;, text: &#x22;The kit's rules, or your AI model from the column map. No rows are sent.&#x22;, code: &#x22;proposal.sql&#x22;, tone: &#x22;ai&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;You read and approve&#x22;, text: &#x22;Read the SQL, edit it if it is wrong, then approve the exact text&#x22;, code: &#x22;proposal.approve()&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;It runs read-only&#x22;, text: &#x22;Through the Exasol MCP server, as the read-only user. At most 1,000 rows come back.&#x22;, code: &#x22;answer = proposal.run()&#x22;, tone: &#x22;db&#x22; },
]"
/>

```python
QUESTION = "How many rows are in each category?"
dataset = nb.dataset(connection, nb.chosen_dataset(None))
nb.example_questions(dataset)                          # questions this column map can answer

proposal = nb.draft_question(connection, dataset, QUESTION)      # the kit's rules: no model
proposal = nb.ask(dataset, QUESTION)                             # your AI model drafts it from the column map
proposal = nb.ask(dataset, QUESTION, proposed_sql="SELECT ...")  # SQL you wrote yourself
```

The three ways differ in who drafts the SQL:

| Way                             | Who drafts                                                                                                                                                         | Sent anywhere                                      |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `nb.draft_question(...)`        | The kit's rules. They match common question shapes: a rate, count, total or average per group, a top N, a trend over time, a filter by year or by a group's value. | Nothing leaves this computer. No model is called.  |
| `nb.ask(dataset, question)`     | Your AI model                                                                                                                                                      | The approved column map and the question. No rows. |
| `nb.ask(..., proposed_sql=...)` | You                                                                                                                                                                | Nothing                                            |

The rules drafter needs no model. `nb.ask` needs one, which you set up with `nb.model_setup()`. Without a model, `nb.ask` stops and says to pass `proposed_sql=` with SQL you wrote. To set up a model, see [Set up Exasol](/data-scientist/set-up/ai-and-langfuse).

### Answers come from the semantic model [#answers-come-from-the-semantic-model]

When a semantic model covers your data, your AI model answers from it. It is shown the model's metrics and dimensions, writes Semantic SQL over the published view, and Exasol Semantic Views compiles that into the plain SQL you read and approve. An AI client over MCP uses the same definitions, so the notebook and the client give the same number for the same question.

Measured: for *revenue by region*, the draft `SELECT region, total_amount FROM SEM_XSRC_TEST.ORDER_LINES GROUP BY region` compiled to a `SUM(AMOUNT)` over `AMAZON.ORDER_LINES` with a `LEFT JOIN` to the state table, the join the model defines. A draft naming a metric the model does not have was refused (`SEMANTIC_QUERY_020`).

The proposal says which model answered and shows the Semantic SQL under *What the model assumed*. If no model covers the data, or the question cannot be put in the model's terms, the SQL is drafted from the approved column map and the proposal says so under *Check before you approve*.

## Read, edit and approve [#read-edit-and-approve]

Read the proposal, and edit it if it is wrong:

```python
proposal.edit("SELECT ...")      # replaces the SQL and removes any approval
```

Approve it, then run it:

```python
proposal.approve()
answer = proposal.run()
```

In the notebook, set `APPROVE_SQL = True` in the Ask cell and run it again. Nothing runs before approval.

Only the exact text you approved runs. `run()` checks the text against the approval. Any change after approval, including an edit, means the query must be approved again.

Each approval adds a line to the workflow log with the question, the approved SQL, its digest and the column map version. Each run adds a line with the row count.

## What the kit allows [#what-the-kit-allows]

The kit accepts one `SELECT` or `WITH` statement. It refuses a second statement, and any statement that writes, such as `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `CREATE`, `DROP`, `GRANT` or `COPY`.

The query runs through the Exasol MCP server, on the read-only user, and never on the notebook's connection. The server returns at most 1,000 rows. The notebook says so when it returns that many.

## The worked example [#the-worked-example]

The worked example is the question in the notebook: `How many rows are in each category?` on `amazon_sales`. For a rate, the rules drafter's own documentation uses the question `Which category has the highest cancellation rate?` on the same table.

Read the SQL the kit returns before you approve it. The repository does not record the SQL or the answer for either question. To see the SQL the kit drafts, draft the question and read the proposal's SQL. Drafting is not approval, so nothing runs:

```python
proposal = nb.draft_question(connection, dataset, "Which category has the highest cancellation rate?")
proposal.sql
```

Check the figures against the SQL yourself.

Back to [Explore and understand](/data-scientist/explore). Previous: [Compare groups and trends](/data-scientist/explore/compare-groups). Next: [Is my data sent anywhere?](/data-scientist/explore/data-privacy).


# Semantic views (/data-scientist/explore/semantic-views)



A **semantic model** is a named layer over your tables. It says which columns are groups, which are numbers to add up, and how tables link. A question can then name a metric, such as the number of order lines, and a group, such as the month, instead of repeating the formula. The kit publishes the model with **Exasol Semantic Views**, a database add-on that stores the model inside the database. Your AI clients read the same model, so the notebook and the clients give the same answer.

<Flow
  caption="From an approved column map to an answer"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;You approve the map&#x22;, text: &#x22;The schema's column maps are approved&#x22;, code: &#x22;role_review.approve(...)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The kit builds the model&#x22;, text: &#x22;Tables become entities, columns become dimensions and metrics&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The model is published&#x22;, text: &#x22;SEM_<SCHEMA> in the database, with views and metrics&#x22;, code: &#x22;semantic.views&#x22;, tone: &#x22;db&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;You or an AI ask&#x22;, text: &#x22;Semantic SQL names metrics and groups&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.semantic_sql(connection, ...)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;ai&#x22; },
]"
/>

## What the model holds [#what-the-model-holds]

The model's structure follows the column maps:

* A table is an **entity**.
* A link between tables is a **relationship**, many to one, with its key mapping.
* A time, category or flag column is a **dimension**. A time column also gives a `<column>_month` dimension.
* A measure is a **fact**, with the metrics `total_<column>` and `average_<column>`.
* Every table has a row count, `<entity>_count`.
* A sensitive column is never exposed.

The approval publishes a model for the schema, named after the schema. For `AMAZON.ORDER_LINES` that model is published as `SEM_AMAZON`. The model is built from the approved column maps of the schema and its approved links.

## Publish the semantic model [#publish-the-semantic-model]

The quickstart's semantic cell builds a model that can span several tables:

```python
SEMANTIC_NAME = "my_data"
SEMANTIC_TABLES = [dataset.fact_table]        # add tables of other schemas: "VS_LOGISTICS.COURIER_DAILY", "MY_DATA.TARGETS"
SEMANTIC_LINKS = []                           # e.g. "MY_DATA.ORDERS.STATE=VS_LOGISTICS.STATE_LOGISTICS.STATE"
PUBLISH_SEMANTIC = False
semantic = nb.semantic_model(connection, SEMANTIC_NAME, tables=SEMANTIC_TABLES, links=SEMANTIC_LINKS, ai=None,
                             preview=not PUBLISH_SEMANTIC)
semantic
```

With `PUBLISH_SEMANTIC = False` the cell shows what it would build and writes nothing. Set it to `True` and run the cell again to publish. The published schema is named after the model in upper case: `SEM_MY_DATA`. `semantic.views` lists the views it holds.

A model can span any number of schemas: sample datasets, your own files and folders, and connected external sources, which are read live. Every table in it needs an approved column map first.

## Ask the model in Semantic SQL [#ask-the-model-in-semantic-sql]

Semantic SQL is a query over a semantic view. You name metrics and group them by dimensions. Get the exact names from the model first, then write the query:

```python
semantic.fields                       # one row per dimension and metric: view, kind, name, what it is
nb.semantic_sql(connection, """
SELECT <DIMENSION>, <METRIC>
FROM SEM_MY_DATA.<VIEW>
GROUP BY <DIMENSION>
""")
```

Replace the placeholders with names from `semantic.fields`. The metric names follow the pattern `total_<column>` and `average_<column>`, and every table gets a row-count metric. `nb.semantic_sql` switches Semantic SQL on for the session before it runs your query, and it runs the query read-only.

## Measured on a real database [#measured-on-a-real-database]

These results come from a local Exasol Personal database, measured on 12 November 2026. The queries are read-only.

* `exakit marketplace semantic-views` installed Exasol Semantic Views v0.6.1 into the database.
* A model was built over the approved prepared view `EXAKIT_PREPARED.AMAZON__ORDER_LINES` and over `EXAKIT_PREPARED.RETAIL_SIGNALS__CUSTOMER_REVIEWS__PLAIN`, and published. It has 2 views, 20 dimensions and 6 metrics: `amazon_order_lines_count`, `total_qty`, `average_qty`, `total_amount`, `average_amount`, and the reviews' row count.
* The prepared view `EXAKIT_PREPARED.AMAZON__ORDER_LINES` holds 128,969 rows. The raw table `AMAZON.ORDER_LINES` holds 128,975. The view drops 6 order lines that are the same as another line in every column but their row id: see [Cleaned views](/data-scientist/prepare/cleaned-views).

**Counting by month.** The model counts what its view holds:

```sql
SELECT order_date_month, amazon_order_lines_count
FROM SEM_KIT_TEST.AMAZON_ORDER_LINES
GROUP BY order_date_month
```

| `order_date_month` | `amazon_order_lines_count` |
| ------------------ | -------------------------- |
| 2022-03-01         | 171                        |
| 2022-04-01         | 49,065                     |
| 2022-05-01         | 42,037                     |
| 2022-06-01         | 37,696                     |

The four months add up to 128,969, the same as `SELECT COUNT(*)` on the view.

**Counting by category.** Grouping by `category` gives the top rows:

| `category`    | `amazon_order_lines_count` | `total_amount` |
| ------------- | -------------------------- | -------------- |
| Set           | 50,281                     | 39,202,022.03  |
| kurta         | 49,874                     | 21,299,013.70  |
| Western Dress | 15,500                     | 11,216,072.69  |

**A metric the AI proposed.** An AI-style proposal added `cancelled_amount`, the sum of `amount` where `status` is `Cancelled`. Its value is 6,919,284.30. That equals `SELECT SUM(AMOUNT) ... WHERE STATUS = 'Cancelled'` on the table. The proposal also added `cancelled_share`, which is `cancelled_amount / total_amount`. It is 0.088, or 8.8%.

**A metric that does not exist.** A proposed metric that names a fact the model does not have was refused, and the refusal gave the reason.

**Reading from an AI client.** The read-only MCP user, the one AI clients use, read the model's metrics from `SEMANTIC_CATALOG.METRICS`.

**Rebuilding on approval.** Approving a column map rebuilt its schema's model. It also refreshed every multi-source model that the table is in.

Measured values are for this database and these tables. Your numbers differ if your data differs.

## One model across sources [#one-model-across-sources]

In the guided view, open **Understand** and scroll to **Semantic views**. Then:

1. Tick the tables. They are listed with their origin: sample data, your data or an external source. Tick as many as the question needs.
2. Give the model a name, for example `sales_360`.
3. Add the links across schemas, one per line, in the form `SCHEMA.TABLE.COLUMN=SCHEMA.TABLE.KEY`. The approved links inside each schema are used on their own.
4. Tick **Let the AI propose business names, synonyms and metrics**, if you have an AI model set up.
5. Click **Preview**. Read the dimensions and metrics of each view, what the AI proposed, and what was refused and why. Nothing is written yet.
6. Click **Publish the model**.

**Models in the database** lists every model. **Refresh it** rebuilds a model the kit built, from the column maps and links approved since.

## Links across sources [#links-across-sources]

Tables of different sources rarely declare how they join, and the same thing is often named differently: a customer number in one, a client id in another. The kit finds such a link from the values the columns hold. It does not match column names, and it needs no foreign key.

<Flow
  caption="How a link between two sources is found"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;Pick the schemas&#x22;, text: &#x22;Sample data, your files, external sources&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Find the keys&#x22;, text: &#x22;Columns whose every value is present and different&#x22;, code: &#x22;one aggregate per table&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Compare values&#x22;, text: &#x22;Up to 500 values of a column, asked of each key&#x22;, code: &#x22;COUNT ... WHERE key IN (...)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;db&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Count the rows&#x22;, text: &#x22;A text link may miss at most 0.1% of its rows&#x22;, tone: &#x22;db&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;You confirm&#x22;, text: &#x22;Tick or untick each link, then publish&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
]"
/>

In the **Semantic views** card, tick the schemas and click **Find links between them**. In a cell or a terminal:

```python
found_links = nb.find_links(connection, ["AMAZON", "RETAIL_SIGNALS", "VS_LOGISTICS"])
```

```bash
exakit describe --links AMAZON,RETAIL_SIGNALS,VS_LOGISTICS
```

Each link comes back with its evidence. Measured on a real database, between the Amazon sample data and a PostgreSQL source read live:

```text
[high] AMAZON.ORDER_LINES.SHIP_STATE -> VS_LOGISTICS.STATE_LOGISTICS.SHIP_STATE:
       128,921 of 128,942 rows have a value in the key; 21 do not
       (not matching: LAKSHADWEEP, ORISSA, RAJSHTHAN, NL, RAJSTHAN)
```

Only 36 of the 47 different state names match (77%), because 11 are misspelt or abbreviated. Those 11 are 21 rows out of 128,942. The kit counts rows, so the link stands and the misspellings are listed for you to clean.

### What a link's confidence means [#what-a-links-confidence-means]

| Confidence | When                                                                    | What to do                                                   |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| high       | A text column (a code, a name) whose rows are in another table's key    | It is ticked for you. Untick it if the meaning is wrong      |
| low        | A link between two plain number columns                                 | Tick it only if you know the two columns mean the same thing |
| partial    | Text values that only partly match, with more than 0.1% of rows missing | Not a link. Look at the spellings first                      |

Numbers get the low mark for a measured reason. A key that is simply 1, 2, 3 and so on holds every small number. On a database with six schemas, the first version of this search proposed 18 links into one such key: a meter id, a quantity and a count of delayed shipments all "matched" an order line id. So a number column is only considered when it spans at least half the key's range and something else supports it: a similar name, an approved column map that calls it a key or an identifier, or a pair proposed by you or an AI. Even then the data can only contradict such a link, never prove it. Two were still proposed between unrelated order numbers, which is why the last word is yours.

### Let an AI, or an AI client, propose links [#let-an-ai-or-an-ai-client-propose-links]

An AI reads what the columns mean; the search above does not. With **Let the AI help** ticked (or `--ai`), your model proposes pairs from column names, types and notes. It is never sent a value. Each pair is then checked against the data like any other.

An AI client such as Claude Code or Codex does the same with its own reading. It checks a pair with:

```bash
exakit describe --links AMAZON,CRM --link AMAZON.ORDER_LINES.CUST_NO=CRM.CUSTOMERS.CUSTOMER_ID
```

A pair the data contradicts comes back as `[rejected]`.

### What is stored [#what-is-stored]

A link you publish becomes a relationship of the model. Its evidence is stored with it: who proposed it, how many rows matched, and which values did not. Read it back with:

```sql
SELECT SCOPE_NAME, DATA_JSON FROM SEMANTIC_CATALOG.CUSTOM_EXTENSIONS
WHERE MODEL_NAME = 'sales_360' AND VENDOR_NAME = 'exakit'
```

The model also lists each table it is built on and whether it is a table in this database or an external source read live.

### What it costs on large data [#what-it-costs-on-large-data]

Every statement of the search is bounded: one aggregate per table, one `SELECT DISTINCT ... LIMIT 500` per column, one count with a list of values per pair, and at most 400 pairs. Measured: six schemas with 25 tables took 223 statements and about 60 seconds, most of it the live source. Three schemas took 26 statements and 23 seconds.

Queries on the published model were measured on 10,002,745 rows joined to a 30,000-row table:

| Query                                          | Semantic SQL | Hand-written SQL |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ---------------- |
| Group by a category                            | 0.20 s       | 0.13 s           |
| Join, group by priority and month (415 groups) | 0.27 s       | 0.21 s           |
| Join with a filter                             | 0.12 s       | not measured     |

The totals were identical in all 415 groups, and the row counts added up to the table. The SQL the model compiles is one scan of the main table, one `LEFT JOIN` per table a dimension needs (none when the dimensions are the main table's own), and one `GROUP BY`. See it for any query with `EXECUTE SCRIPT SEMANTIC_ADMIN.COMPILE_SQL('<your Semantic SQL>')`.

## The AI proposes the fields [#the-ai-proposes-the-fields]

With `ai=None`, the notebook asks the AI only when a model is set up. The AI proposes business names, comments, synonyms and the metrics people will ask for. It works from names, types, grains, column notes and a category's most frequent values. It never receives a row, and never a sensitive column.

Every metric the AI proposes is checked before the kit offers it. Semantic Views checks it again when the model is built. A refused metric is skipped, and the preview names it. Without a model, the fields keep the names the column maps give.

To set up the AI model, see [Set up Exasol](/data-scientist/set-up/ai-and-langfuse).

## Keep the model current [#keep-the-model-current]

Approving a column map rebuilds every model its table is in. After you add a link or a table, refresh the model yourself:

```python
nb.refresh_semantic(connection, "sales_360")
```

```bash
exakit describe --model sales_360 --refresh
```

Your AI clients read the same model through the Exasol MCP server. The notebook and the clients answer from one meaning.

Back to [Explore and understand](/data-scientist/explore). Previous: [Approve the column map](/data-scientist/explore/approve-the-column-map). Next: [Linked tables](/data-scientist/explore/linked-tables).


# Troubleshooting (/data-scientist/explore/troubleshooting)



Each entry starts with the message or symptom you see. Find it, then read the fix.

<Accordions type="multiple">
  <Accordion title="Why does a notebook say my data is not approved?">
    Explore, Ask and Share read only an approved column map. A step given a draft raises `DescriptorNotApproved`. Open `00_quickstart`, review the map and approve it. The message says the same.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="A step says the column map is not approved">
    The message is a `DescriptorNotApproved` error. Explore, Ask and Share do not read a draft. Open `00_quickstart` and approve the map. This is the same error as the entry above.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Step 1 approved a different dataset after this notebook opened">
    You approved a different dataset in the quickstart while this notebook was open. Run this notebook's first cell again. It switches to the newly approved dataset.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Approval gave a warning about a column">
    A warning about a column that gives the target away is not an error. The column stays in the map and is left out of the model. Read the warning, check the column, and approve. If the column is correct, keep it in the map. The model still leaves it out. For the rule, see [Columns that give the answer away](/data-scientist/prepare/leakage).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="The kit says a value is refused as a target">
    A target must hold 0 and 1, or true and false. A column with other values cannot be predicted. Pick another column, or leave the target empty and explore the data without one.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="A text step is skipped">
    The dataset has no text column. `amazon_sales` and `fraud_transactions` have none, so the text steps skip on them and say so.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="A step is skipped: no date, no target, no group">
    The step needs a column the approved map does not give it. The step prints which role is missing. Set the slot in the column map, or use a dataset that has the column.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="A question gets no answer, or an error">
    The rules drafter drafts only the question shapes it knows. Rephrase the question, or write the SQL yourself with `proposed_sql=` and approve it. If the query cannot run, the message says why. If the MCP server does not answer, run `exakit mcp-doctor`.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="A semantic model publish failed">
    The approval still stands, and the message says why. Retry with `exakit describe <id> --comments`, or refresh the model with `nb.refresh_semantic(connection, "<name>")` once the cause is fixed.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Where is my work saved?">
    Under `~/.exasol-starter-kit`:

    * Column maps and their versions, in `descriptors/`.
    * Semantic model definitions, in `semantic/`, so a refresh rebuilds a model the same way.
    * Workflow logs, in `workflows/`. See [Get the data](/data-scientist/get-the-data) for the workflow log.
    * Hand-off bundles, written by the share stage.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Find what a cell ran">
    ```python
    nb.show_sql()                              # the SQL the last query ran
    nb.workflow_log(nb.current_workflow())     # everything this workflow did
    ```
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do I need an AI model?">
    No. Every step runs without one. A model is used only to draft SQL in Ask and to sort texts into themes, and both are off until you turn them on. Ask also has a drafter with no model: `nb.draft_question`.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why is a column never charted or sent to a model?">
    The kit marks a column as sensitive when its values look like personal data: e-mail addresses, phone numbers, IBANs or postcodes. A sensitive column is never charted, grouped or sent to a model, and it is never exposed in the semantic model. The card says so beside the column. A sensitive column cannot be the target, a category or an entity.
  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

Back to [Explore and understand](/data-scientist/explore). Previous: [Is my data sent anywhere?](/data-scientist/explore/data-privacy).


# The checks (/data-scientist/evaluate/checks)



Three checks sit behind the evaluation. The first two print what they find and return it as a value. The third returns true or false.

## The checks [#the-checks]

* **`nb.leakage_check`** lists the columns that give the answer away. It tests each column that is not the target, a key, an identifier or free text. The approval runs it too. See [Leakage](/data-scientist/evaluate/leakage).
* **`nb.data_checks`** reports repeated keys and ids, exact copies of a row, empty cells, placeholder values such as `Unknown Device`, and a rare label. The repeated keys and copies can inflate a score when a copied row lands on both sides of the split. The data checks are documented on the [data checks reference](/data-scientist/development/reference/data-checks) page.
* **`nb.check_model_compatibility(conn, model_version, alias="PYTHON3", model_path="model.pkl")`** checks a pickled scikit-learn model before anything is scored in the database. It refuses when the model's scikit-learn version differs from the version in the database's Python container. The Data Scientist notebooks do not pickle or score models, so this check belongs to the ML Engineer's scoring notebook.

## What to do with a finding [#what-to-do-with-a-finding]

Each finding says what it does to a result. The kit does not fix the table or drop rows for you. Decide what to do, make the change in your own cleaned view or column map, and run the check again. The cleaned views are on [Prepare](/data-scientist/prepare).

Back to [Evaluate](/data-scientist/evaluate). Next: [When it goes wrong](/data-scientist/evaluate/troubleshooting).


# Comparing models (/data-scientist/evaluate/comparing-models)



The kit does not compute a p-value, a confidence interval or a significance test. A p-value is a number that says how likely a gap this size would be by chance alone. A confidence interval is a range the true score probably falls in. The kit gives you the parts you need to judge a difference yourself.

## What you have to judge a difference [#what-you-have-to-judge-a-difference]

* **The spread across folds.** `cv_sd` on the board shows how much a model's score moves between folds. A gap between two models that is smaller than that spread is not a reliable difference.
* **The model rule.** The lab picks the simpler model when two are within 0.01 of each other. That is a rule for choosing, not a test that the gap is real. See [The models the lab tries](/data-scientist/model/the-models).
* **The feature rule.** A verdict of `helps` needs a rise of 0.005 in cross-validation and no fall of more than 0.002 on the held-out rows. That is a rule of thumb. See [Feature ideas](/data-scientist/model/feature-ideas).
* **Small groups.** Groups with fewer than 30 rows are not compared. This applies to the group and trend notes. See [The readout notes](/data-scientist/evaluate/readout-notes).
* **The held-out size.** The warnings for a small held-out set are on [Hold-out](/data-scientist/evaluate/hold-out).

## If you need a p-value or an interval [#if-you-need-a-p-value-or-an-interval]

Compute it in your own code, on the rows you have, and say in your write-up that the kit did not compute it. `cv` is the mean of the fold scores and `cv_sd` is their standard deviation, so the two are a starting point. They are not a full analysis.

Back to [Evaluate](/data-scientist/evaluate). Next: [The readout notes](/data-scientist/evaluate/readout-notes).


# Hold-out (/data-scientist/evaluate/hold-out)



Every model in the lab is trained on the same training rows and scored on the same held-out rows. The held-out rows are the test. Keeping them apart is the only way to see how a model does on rows it has not seen.

## Hold-out: how rows are kept apart [#hold-out-how-rows-are-kept-apart]

<Flow
  caption="Three ways to split, chosen from the column map and your settings"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;A date in the column map&#x22;, text: &#x22;The default split is by time: the oldest rows learn, the newest rows are tested&#x22;, code: 'split_method=&#x22;time&#x22;', tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;No date&#x22;, text: &#x22;The default split is random, with a fixed seed. Yes or no is stratified.&#x22;, code: 'split_method=&#x22;random&#x22;', tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;You name a group column&#x22;, text: &#x22;Whole groups go to one side. No group is on both sides.&#x22;, code: 'split_method=&#x22;group&#x22;, split_group=&#x22;...&#x22;', tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
]"
/>

| Split method | When the lab uses it                       | What the held-out rows are                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `time`       | The default when the column map has a date | The newest rows. The model learns from the oldest and is tested on the newest, so it never sees the future. Cross-validation uses time-ordered folds (`TimeSeriesSplit`). |
| `random`     | The default when there is no date          | A random share, with a fixed seed. For yes or no it is stratified, so both sides keep the same share of 1s.                                                               |
| `group`      | You name a group column with `split_group` | Whole groups. No group appears on both sides.                                                                                                                             |

Two settings shape the split. `train_pct` is the share used for training: 50 to 90, and 75 by default. `folds` is the number of cross-validation folds on the training side: 5 by default.

The kit warns when the held-out set is too small to trust:

* For yes or no: fewer than 30 rows with a 1 held out.
* For a number to predict: fewer than 100 rows held out.

## The baseline's score on amazon_sales [#the-baselines-score-on-amazon_sales]

The notebook holds out a quarter of the rows, scores the model on them, and prints the note:

```python
roc_auc = roc_auc_score(test_labels, model.predict_proba(test_features)[:, 1])
print(f"ROC AUC on the held-out quarter: {roc_auc:.3f}")
nb.note_model(roc_auc, dataset, len(model_rows), label_values.mean())
```

The notebook's hold-out is a stratified random split with `random_state=0`. The same rows are held out on every rerun, as long as the table has not changed.

The notebook baseline splits at random, even though `amazon_sales` has a date. The lab splits by time. The two scores are measured on different rows, so do not compare them as if they were one test.

## The lab's hold-out on amazon_sales [#the-labs-hold-out-on-amazon_sales]

The lab reads the newest 50,000 rows, since the table has 128,975. It learns from the oldest 75% of those and is tested on the newest 25%. The output line reads: "The oldest 75% by ORDER_DATE to learn from, the newest 25% to test on. The model never sees the future."

## The hold-out on fraud_transactions [#the-hold-out-on-fraud_transactions]

With no date, the lab holds out rows at random, stratified so both sides keep the same share of fraud. The table has 50,000 distinct `TRANSACTION_ID` values across 51,000 rows, so 1,000 ids repeat. A repeated row that lands on both sides of the split can make the score look better than it is. `nb.data_checks` reports repeated ids and exact copies. Read that report before you trust a score on this table.

Back to [Evaluate](/data-scientist/evaluate). Next: [Metrics](/data-scientist/evaluate/metrics).


# Evaluate (/data-scientist/evaluate)



Evaluation answers one question: how well will this model do on rows it has not seen? A score on the rows it learned from says little, because a model can memorise them. The kit holds rows out before it trains, reports the metric that fits your task, and warns you about the traps it can detect: columns that give the answer away, rare answers, and held-out sets that are too small. It does not run significance tests. The page on comparing models says what to do about that.

<Flow
  caption="Hold rows out, train on the rest, score the unseen rows, read the result"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;Hold rows out&#x22;, text: &#x22;The newest rows (time), a random share (stratified for yes or no), or whole groups&#x22;, code: 'nb.model_lab(connection, dataset, &#x22;predict_yes_no&#x22;, split_method=&#x22;time&#x22;)', tone: &#x22;kit&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/evaluate/hold-out&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Train on the rest&#x22;, text: &#x22;Cross-validation on the training rows chooses the model&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/model/the-models&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Score the unseen rows&#x22;, text: &#x22;The held-out rows are scored once, with the metrics for the task&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/evaluate/metrics&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Read the note&#x22;, text: &#x22;The kit says what the number means, in words&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.note_model(roc_auc, dataset, rows=len(model_rows))&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/evaluate/readout-notes&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;You decide&#x22;, text: &#x22;Is the score real? Check the leakage, the baseline and the size of the held-out set&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
]"
/>

<Flow
  caption="When the score looks too good"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;A near-perfect score&#x22;, text: &#x22;Treat it as a warning, not good news&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Look for leakage&#x22;, text: &#x22;Columns whose values decide the answer on their own&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.leakage_check(connection, dataset)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/evaluate/leakage&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Leave them out&#x22;, text: &#x22;The baseline and the lab skip the flagged columns&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Train again on the same split&#x22;, text: &#x22;The seed is fixed, so the two scores compare fairly&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
]"
/>

## Where you do it [#where-you-do-it]

| Guided view                                                                                                    | Notebook code                                                                                                                                       | Terminal                               |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `01_explore`: the **Build a model** card runs the same lab, and its results show the leaderboard and the pick. | The cells **Score on unseen rows** and **The model lab (optional)** in `01_explore`. `lab.board`, `lab.importance` and `lab.note` hold the results. | None. Scoring happens in the notebook. |

## How we used it [#how-we-used-it]

On `amazon_sales`, the notebook baseline is scored on a quarter of the rows it did not train on, with ROC AUC. The notebook prints the score. This repository does not record a value for it, so these pages quote none.

Two results are measured on the real database and are the basis of the warnings:

* **The leakage trap.** `STATUS` is `Cancelled` on exactly the 18,332 rows whose `CANCELLED` is 1. A model that reads `STATUS` learns the answer it was given. See [Leakage](/data-scientist/evaluate/leakage).
* **The rare answer.** `fraud_transactions` has 2,510 fraud rows out of 51,000 (4.9%). A model that always says "not fraud" is about 95% accurate, so accuracy is the wrong score. See [Rare answers](/data-scientist/evaluate/rare-answers).

## In this stage [#in-this-stage]

<Cards>
  <Card title="Hold-out: how rows are kept apart" href="/data-scientist/evaluate/hold-out" description="The time, random and group splits, and the warnings for a small held-out set" />

  <Card title="Metrics" href="/data-scientist/evaluate/metrics" description="The score each task uses, and what the board's columns mean" />

  <Card title="Reading ROC AUC" href="/data-scientist/evaluate/roc-auc" description="What the number means, and what the note says for each range" />

  <Card title="Rare answers" href="/data-scientist/evaluate/rare-answers" description="Why accuracy fails when the answer is rare, and which score the kit uses instead" />

  <Card title="Leakage" href="/data-scientist/evaluate/leakage" description="Columns that give the answer away, how the kit finds them, and how to check" />

  <Card title="Comparing models" href="/data-scientist/evaluate/comparing-models" description="What the kit does not test, and what to do about a difference" />

  <Card title="The readout notes" href="/data-scientist/evaluate/readout-notes" description="The plain-language notes under each result" />

  <Card title="The checks" href="/data-scientist/evaluate/checks" description="The functions that check the data and the model before you rely on them" />

  <Card title="When it goes wrong" href="/data-scientist/evaluate/troubleshooting" description="Warnings and suspicious scores, and what to do about them" />
</Cards>

## What you have at the end [#what-you-have-at-the-end]

A score on rows the model did not learn from, what that score means in words, the list of what the model leans on, and the warnings the kit raised. The score shows that the inputs carry signal about the outcome. It does not show that any input causes it. Next, share the result in [Communicate and deploy](/data-scientist/communicate).

<StageNav n="6" />


# Leakage (/data-scientist/evaluate/leakage)



Leakage means a column carries the answer. Its values are written after the outcome happens, so a model that reads it learns the answer it was given, not a pattern that works on new rows. A model with leakage looks excellent on the rows it learned from and fails on new rows.

## The case on amazon_sales [#the-case-on-amazon_sales]

`STATUS` is the classic trap. The dataset README says `STATUS`, `COURIER_STATUS`, `QTY` and `AMOUNT` all change once an order is cancelled. So a cancelled order says so in `STATUS`, and the target `CANCELLED` is 1 for that order.

This was measured on the sample table, `AMAZON.ORDER_LINES`, on 12 November 2026. The queries are read-only:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AMAZON.ORDER_LINES WHERE STATUS = 'Cancelled';                    -- 18,332
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AMAZON.ORDER_LINES WHERE STATUS = 'Cancelled' AND CANCELLED = 1;  -- 18,332
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AMAZON.ORDER_LINES WHERE CANCELLED = 1;                           -- 18,332
```

The three counts are equal. Every row with `CANCELLED` = 1 has `STATUS` = `Cancelled`, and no other row does. So `STATUS` gives the target away completely. A model that reads it will look perfect.

The notebook's comment puts the problem this way: such a column "predicts the target perfectly on old rows and fails on new rows."

## How the kit finds it [#how-the-kit-finds-it]

`nb.leakage_check` flags a column when all of these hold:

* It has 2 to 50 distinct values. Columns with more values are not tested.
* Each of its values is nearly always 1 (at least 99% of its rows) or nearly always 0 (at least 99%).
* Those values together cover at least 95% of all rows, and they hold at least 90% of the 1s.

For `STATUS`, the value `Cancelled` has a 1 in every row, and every other status has a 0 in every row. So every value is pure, the pure values cover all the rows, and they hold all the 1s. The rule flags `STATUS`.

Its message, as `nb.leakage_check` prints it, has this form:

```
- STATUS gives CANCELLED away: CANCELLED is 1 whenever STATUS is 'Cancelled'. It was probably written after the outcome - leave it out of any model.
```

## What the kit does with a flagged column [#what-the-kit-does-with-a-flagged-column]

The kit guards against leakage in three places.

* **The approval warns.** When you approve the column map, the card says `STATUS` gives the answer away, because it is filled in after the outcome, and that the model step leaves it out.
* **The baseline never reads it.** The notebook baseline skips a flagged category or entity. On `amazon_sales` it reads only the category, the state and the month.
* **The lab leaves it out.** `lab_data.left_out` lists `STATUS` with the reason "gives the answer away".

The quickstart says the check flags `STATUS` on `amazon_sales`. Confirm that on your data, because the check depends on the values present in your table.

## Check it yourself [#check-it-yourself]

```python
leaking = nb.leakage_check(connection, dataset)   # the columns the kit flags
lab_data = nb.lab_data(connection, dataset)
print(lab_data.left_out)                          # every column left out, and why
```

## What the check cannot see [#what-the-check-cannot-see]

The check tests only columns with 2 to 50 distinct values. A numeric column such as `AMOUNT` usually has many more values, so the check skips it. The README says `AMOUNT` changes after a cancellation, so the check cannot be the last word on it.

Two other checks cover the gap:

* **Look at `lab.importance` after every run.** If a column you suspect is at the top, it is a lead to read.
* **Leave it out with `leaks=`.** For example: `leaks = nb.leakage_check(connection, dataset) + ["AMOUNT"]`, then pass `leaks=leaks` to `nb.model_lab`. The model lab page has the full example.

For a number to predict, the lab also drops any measure whose correlation with the target is above 0.98, because it moves with the target almost exactly.

Back to [Evaluate](/data-scientist/evaluate). Next: [Comparing models](/data-scientist/evaluate/comparing-models).


# Metrics (/data-scientist/evaluate/metrics)



Each model is scored with the metric for its task. The metric the lab picks by comes first in the table. The board shows the other columns as well.

## Metrics [#metrics]

| Task                | The metric the lab picks by                                                       | Also on the held-out rows                                               |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Predict yes or no   | ROC AUC. PR AUC when the rarer answer is under 5%.                                | ROC AUC, PR AUC and F1 at a 0.5 cut-off                                 |
| Predict a number    | R squared                                                                         | R squared, mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) |
| Find natural groups | Silhouette score: how well each row fits its own group compared with the next one | The number of groups tried, and the score for each                      |
| Find unusual rows   | None is scored. You set the share to flag (`contamination`, 2% by default).       | The flagged count, the share, and what sets the flagged rows apart      |

In plain words:

* **ROC AUC** is the chance that the model gives a row with a 1 a higher score than a row with a 0. It is explained on [Reading ROC AUC](/data-scientist/evaluate/roc-auc).
* **PR AUC** is the average precision score: how well the model's top-ranked rows contain the rare 1s. It is the one to read when 1s are rare.
* **F1** combines how many flagged rows are right and how many real 1s are found, at one cut-off (0.5 here).
* **R squared** is the share of the spread in the number that the model explains. A value of 0 means no better than the average.
* **MAE** is the average size of the miss, in the number's own units. **RMSE** is similar, but it punishes large misses more.
* **Silhouette score** is how close each row sits to its own group, compared with the nearest other group.

## The columns on the board [#the-columns-on-the-board]

* `cv` is the mean cross-validated score for the metric the lab picks by.
* `cv_sd` is how much that score varies across folds. Read it before you compare two models.
* `held` is the held-out score for the same metric.

The board's other columns (`roc_auc`, `pr_auc`, `f1`, `r2`, `mae`, `rmse`) are the held-out values for each model.

```python
lab.board    # one row per model: cv, cv_sd, held, and the other held-out metrics
```

Back to [Evaluate](/data-scientist/evaluate). Next: [Reading ROC AUC](/data-scientist/evaluate/roc-auc).


# Rare answers (/data-scientist/evaluate/rare-answers)



When one answer is rare, a model can look good by always giving the common answer. This page shows the numbers from the two sample datasets, and what the kit does about it.

## Why accuracy misleads [#why-accuracy-misleads]

`fraud_transactions` has 51,000 rows, and 2,510 of them are fraud (4.9%). A model that always says "not fraud" is right on 48,490 rows, which is about 95% accuracy. It finds no fraud at all. A score that rewards that model is useless for finding fraud.

The data check reports the same thing. `nb.data_checks` prints a finding named "rare label", and the sentence says what a model that always answers the common value achieves.

## Two thresholds, for two different jobs [#two-thresholds-for-two-different-jobs]

The kit uses two cut-offs for the share of the rarer answer. They do different jobs, so the numbers differ.

| Where                                     | Threshold | What happens                                  | `amazon_sales` (14.2%) | `fraud_transactions` (4.9%) |
| ----------------------------------------- | --------- | --------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | --------------------------- |
