| `nb.data_checks` (the rare-label finding) | Under 10% | The label is reported as rare                 | Not reported           | Reported as rare            |
| The model lab                             | Under 5%  | The lab scores with PR AUC instead of ROC AUC | ROC AUC                | PR AUC                      |

## What PR AUC is [#what-pr-auc-is]

PR AUC is the average precision score. It ranks the rows by the model's score and asks how many of the rows at the top are real 1s, averaged over the ranking. It is only interested in finding the 1s, so it does not reward a model for being right about the many 0s. The lab records the reason in `lab.run.notes`: "The 1s are rare, so the score is PR AUC, which focuses on finding them."

## What the readout note says [#what-the-readout-note-says]

For ROC AUC, `nb.note_model` names the always-common guess and its accuracy as the baseline to beat. The note also says that accuracy is not the score when the answer is rare.

## Repeated rows can also inflate a rare-answer score [#repeated-rows-can-also-inflate-a-rare-answer-score]

`fraud_transactions` has 51,000 rows and 50,000 distinct `TRANSACTION_ID` values. So 1,000 ids appear twice. When a repeated copy lands on both sides of the split, the model can score a row it has already learned. `nb.data_checks` reports repeated ids and exact copies. Read that report before you judge a score on this table. The split is on [Hold-out](/data-scientist/evaluate/hold-out).

Back to [Evaluate](/data-scientist/evaluate). Next: [Leakage](/data-scientist/evaluate/leakage).


# The readout notes (/data-scientist/evaluate/readout-notes)



The readout helpers print a plain-language note under each result and return it as text. Nothing is computed that the result does not hold. If a note would need a number the result lacks, it leaves the sentence out.

## The readout notes [#the-readout-notes]

* **`nb.note_groups`** is for a per-group result. It says what one row is, the overall figure, the highest and the lowest group, which groups have too few rows to trust (fewer than 30), and that a difference between groups is not a cause.
* **`nb.note_trend`** is for a per-period result. It names the busiest period and the highest and lowest percentage, leaves out periods with fewer than 30 rows, and says that a change over time shows when something moved, not why.
* **`nb.note_model`** is for the small model's score. It says what the score means in words (the ranges are on [Reading ROC AUC](/data-scientist/evaluate/roc-auc)), how many rows the model learned from, and the baseline to beat.

The 30-row limit is one constant, `SMALL`, in `readout.py`. It is the same for groups and periods.

## Where the words come from [#where-the-words-come-from]

The notes take their words from the column map. The grain "one row per order line" makes the note say "order lines", and the count column is named `ORDER_LINES`. Three helpers do that naming:

* `nb.name` gives a column's readable name.
* `nb.count_name` gives the name of the count column for the dataset.
* `nb.noun` gives the plural noun for one row.

The note is printed under the table and also returned as a string, so you can copy it next to the figures in a report.

Back to [Evaluate](/data-scientist/evaluate). Next: [The checks](/data-scientist/evaluate/checks).


# Reading ROC AUC (/data-scientist/evaluate/roc-auc)



ROC AUC is the score the lab uses for a yes-or-no prediction when the rarer answer is 5% or more. It is a number from 0 to 1.

## Reading ROC AUC [#reading-roc-auc]

ROC AUC is the chance that the model gives a row with a 1 a higher score than a row with a 0. Pick one row that has a 1 and one that has a 0 at random. A score of 0.5 means the model ranks them correctly only half the time, which is guessing. A score of 1.0 means it always ranks the 1 higher.

The readout note turns the number into words:

| ROC AUC           | What the note says                                         |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Below 0.6         | About as good as guessing                                  |
| 0.6 to below 0.7  | A weak signal                                              |
| 0.7 to below 0.85 | A useful signal                                            |
| 0.85 and above    | A strong signal. Check that it is not too good to be true. |

The note also says that 50% is guessing, and that accuracy is not the score when the answer is rare.

## What the lab does with it [#what-the-lab-does-with-it]

* The lab's own `baseline` model always gives the same answer, so its ROC AUC is 0.5. Any real model should score above it.
* The lab scores each model by cross-validated ROC AUC and picks from those scores (the rule is on [The models the lab tries](/data-scientist/model/the-models)). It reports the held-out ROC AUC beside each one.
* On `amazon_sales`, the rarer answer is 14.2% of rows, so the metric is ROC AUC. On `fraud_transactions`, the rarer answer is 4.9%, so the metric is PR AUC instead. See [Rare answers](/data-scientist/evaluate/rare-answers).

## Where the note comes from [#where-the-note-comes-from]

`nb.note_model` writes the note. Its wording is in `readout.py`, in the function of the same name. The ranges in the table above are the ones coded there. Nothing in the note is a statistical test.

Back to [Evaluate](/data-scientist/evaluate). Next: [Rare answers](/data-scientist/evaluate/rare-answers).


# Troubleshooting (/data-scientist/evaluate/troubleshooting)



Each entry quotes the warning or describes the score you see.

<Accordions type="multiple">
  <Accordion title="Only a few rows with a 1 are held out">
    The warning reads "Only N rows with a 1 are held out, so the held-out score is shaky". It appears when fewer than 30 rows with a 1 are held out. Lower `train_pct` (50 is the lowest it accepts), so more rows are held out, or use more data. See [Hold-out](/data-scientist/evaluate/hold-out).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="One side of the split has only one answer">
    The error reads "One side of the split has only one answer, so no score can be computed". No score can be computed when one side has only 0s or only 1s. Change the split to `split_method="random"`, which is stratified for yes or no.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="The score jumped almost to perfect">
    The idea you tried scored above 0.98 on the held-out rows, and the verdict is `suspicious`. The kit says "The score jumped almost to perfect. That usually means the idea gives the answer away. Don't keep it." Do not keep it. For the whole model, run `nb.leakage_check` and read `lab_data.left_out`. See [Leakage](/data-scientist/evaluate/leakage).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="A near-perfect score from the start">
    Treat it as a leak until proved otherwise. Check the importance list, the leakage check and the column map. A score that is near perfect on the first run is almost never the model's real skill. The [leakage page](/data-scientist/evaluate/leakage) shows how a column like `STATUS` produces one.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="The held-out score is worse than cross-validation">
    A gap in either direction can be noise, especially with a small held-out set. Look at the number of rows held out, and at `cv_sd`, before you read anything into the gap. See [Comparing models](/data-scientist/evaluate/comparing-models).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="The score looks good, but the table has repeated ids">
    On `fraud_transactions`, 1,000 ids appear twice. A copy on both sides of the split can make the held-out score look better than it is. Run `nb.data_checks` and read the repeated-id finding. See [Rare answers](/data-scientist/evaluate/rare-answers).
  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

Back to [Evaluate](/data-scientist/evaluate).


# Add a command (/data-scientist/development/add-a-command)



<Steps>
  <Step>
    ### Write the helper [#write-the-helper]

    Add a function to a module in `notebook/package/exakit_nb/`, with a docstring. The first sentence becomes its one-line summary here; the rest becomes its reference text. Indented lines in a docstring are shown as code.

    Export it: import it in `exakit_nb/__init__.py` and add its name to `__all__`.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Put it in a notebook [#put-it-in-a-notebook]

    Add the call to the code section of the notebook it belongs to, guarded by a variable when it is optional:

    ```python
    if ADD_ON:
        nb.addon_ready(ADD_ON)
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Give a card a button for it [#give-a-card-a-button-for-it]

    Add one entry to `actions.ACTIONS` in `exakit_guide/actions.py`: the code and the notebook it belongs to. Have the screen call `actions.run(...)`.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Regenerate [#regenerate]

    ```bash
    python3 tools/notebooks.py --marimo     # the .ipynb and Marimo notebooks
    python3 tools/nb_docs.py                # the command reference
    ```

    The new helper now has an entry in its module's reference page and a row in [All commands](/data-scientist/development/reference). `nb.docs(nb.your_helper)` opens it once the site is rebuilt.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Test [#test]

    ```bash
    python3 -m unittest tests.test_notebook_guide tests.test_notebook_helpers tests.test_notebook_docs
    ```
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Callout>
  A whole new module gets its own reference page automatically, titled from its file name. Give it a proper title and a place in the order by adding one line to `PAGES` in `tools/nb_docs.py`.
</Callout>


# These docs (/data-scientist/development/docs-site)



## How it works [#how-it-works]

* **Source:** MDX pages in `notebook/docs/content/docs/`, one folder per persona. The folder layout is the sidebar; each folder's `meta.json` sets its title and page order, and a persona's folder is marked `"root": true`, which makes it an entry in the list at the top of the sidebar.
* **Build:** a static site built with Node on a maintainer's machine. Users never need Node.
* **Shipped:** the built files, in `notebook/docs/site/`, travel with the kit.
* **Served:** `nb.docs()` serves that folder from the kit's own Python, on this computer only.

Search runs in the browser on an index inside the site. It forgives typos, matches as you type and needs no internet.

## Change a page [#change-a-page]

<Steps>
  <Step>
    ### Edit [#edit]

    Edit an `.mdx` file, or add one and list it in its folder's `meta.json`. Each page starts with:

    ```text
    ---
    title: Page title
    description: One sentence that says what the page covers.
    ---
    ```

    `Callout`, `Tabs`, `Steps`, `Cards` and `Accordions` are available on every page without imports.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Preview while you write [#preview-while-you-write]

    ```bash
    npm install
    ```

    ```bash
    npm run dev
    ```

    Run both in `notebook/docs`. The site is at `http://localhost:3000/docs` and reloads on every save.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Build and publish [#build-and-publish]

    ```bash
    npm run build
    ```

    ```bash
    python3 tools/nb_docs.py --publish
    ```

    The first writes `notebook/docs/out`; the second copies it to `notebook/docs/site` and stamps it with a digest of the sources.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Check [#check]

    ```bash
    python3 tools/nb_docs.py --check
    ```

    It fails when a generated page is stale, or when the shipped site was built from older sources than the ones in the repository.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Pages you do not edit [#pages-you-do-not-edit]

Everything under a persona's `reference/` folder is generated from the docstrings in `exakit_nb` by `python3 tools/nb_docs.py`. To change a command's text, change its docstring and run the tool.

## Links [#links]

Link to a page by its address, without the `/docs` prefix and without `.mdx`: `/data-scientist/concepts/descriptor`. Link to a command by its page and name: `/data-scientist/development/reference/describe#describe`. A test fails on a link that leads nowhere.


# How it fits together (/data-scientist/development/how-it-fits)



## Three layers [#three-layers]

| Layer           | Where                                                    | What it owns                                                                  |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The kit         | `setup/`, the `exakit` command                           | The database, connections, loading, connectors, add-ons, the describe service |
| The helpers     | `notebook/package/exakit_nb/` (`import exakit.nb as nb`) | One Python call for each thing a notebook does                                |
| The guided view | `notebook/package/exakit_guide/` (`exakit.guide`)        | Cards that call the helpers; UI only                                          |

A notebook is cells that call the helpers. A card is a form that calls the same helpers. Neither talks to the database on its own.

## The helpers [#the-helpers]

`exakit.nb` exports about 110 names, listed in [All commands](/data-scientist/development/reference). The rules they follow:

* **The connection comes from the kit.** `nb.connect()` opens it from the kit's encrypted store. No helper prints or returns a host, a user or a password.
* **The kit does the work.** Describing a table is the kit's describe service; loading is `exakit data-load`; connecting a source is `exakit connect`. The helpers call these, they do not reimplement them.
* **SQL is shown.** `nb.sql` records the statement, `nb.show_sql()` prints it, and the workflow logs it.
* **Reads are live.** `nb.components()`, `nb.addons()`, `nb.connectors()` and the rest ask the kit when called.

## The guided view [#the-guided-view]

```text
notebook/package/exakit_guide/
  actions.py     every action: one or more lines of exakit.nb code, and its notebook
  session.py     the notebook's namespace the actions run in
  card.py        the widget; a button's code comes from its action
  screens/       one module per page (home, understand, explore, ask, share): UI only
  static/        card.js and card.css: the renderer, no facts
```

`actions.code(id, **values)` is the exact cell text. `actions.run(id, **values)` runs that text in the notebook's namespace and logs it. A screen changes nothing except through `actions.run`, which is why **Code** can always show what a card did.

## Rules the tests enforce [#rules-the-tests-enforce]

* An action's call exists in its notebook's code section, and calls something `exakit.nb` exports.
* No screen names a dataset, connector, add-on or notebook. Those are read from the kit.
* No action shows a secret: a key is bound at run time, never written into the code.
* Every exported helper has a page in these docs, and every link in them leads somewhere.

## Notebooks [#notebooks]

Sources are `notebook/notebooks/<persona>/<NN>_<name>.py` in jupytext percent format. The `.ipynb` and the Marimo version are built from them:

```bash
python3 tools/notebooks.py --marimo            # rebuild
python3 tools/notebooks.py --check --marimo    # fail when a built file is stale
```

## Further reading [#further-reading]

* [pyexasol](https://github.com/exasol/pyexasol), the Python driver that `nb.connect()` opens, with its [documentation](https://exasol.github.io/pyexasol/master/index.html).
* [exapump](https://github.com/exasol-labs/exapump), the command-line client the kit uses for SQL and loading.
* [Exasol MCP server](https://exasol.github.io/mcp-server/main/index.html), the server behind the AI clients, and its [repository](https://github.com/exasol/mcp-server).
* [virtual-schemas](https://github.com/exasol/virtual-schemas), behind the `VS_<NAME>` schemas of external sources.
* [Exasol Personal](https://github.com/exasol/exasol-personal), the local database the kit deploys.
* [Security](/security), how the layers above handle credentials, the network and models.


# Development (/data-scientist/development)



This section is for people who build on the kit, or who want the commands behind the notebooks. The stage pages tell you what to do. These pages tell you how it works underneath.

<Cards>
  <Card title="How it fits together" href="/data-scientist/development/how-it-fits">
    The three layers, and the rules that keep them honest.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Command reference" href="/data-scientist/development/reference">
    Every public helper of 

    `exakit.nb`

    , generated from its docstrings.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Where things live" href="/data-scientist/development/where-things-live">
    The files and folders the notebooks read and write.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Add a command" href="/data-scientist/development/add-a-command">
    Write a helper, wire it to a card, and get its page.
  </Card>

  <Card title="These docs" href="/data-scientist/development/docs-site">
    How this site is written, built and shipped.
  </Card>
</Cards>

## How the pieces fit [#how-the-pieces-fit]

Three layers do the work. Each has one job.

| Layer           | Where it lives                                               | What it owns                                                                     |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The kit         | `setup/` and the `exakit` command                            | The database, connections, loading, connectors, add-ons and the describe service |
| The helpers     | `notebook/package/exakit_nb/`, imported as `exakit.nb`       | One Python call for each thing a notebook does                                   |
| The guided view | `notebook/package/exakit_guide/`, imported as `exakit.guide` | The cards, which call the helpers. They have no logic of their own.              |

A notebook is cells that call the helpers. A card is a form that calls the same helpers. Neither talks to the database on its own.

Every step follows the same path, whether you run a cell or click a card:

<Flow
  caption="From a notebook cell to the database"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;Notebook cell&#x22;, text: &#x22;Or a card button, which runs the same code&#x22;, code: 'dataset = nb.dataset(connection, &#x22;amazon_sales&#x22;)', tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;exakit.nb helper&#x22;, text: &#x22;Builds the SQL from the approved roles, shows it and logs the step&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Kit service or CLI&#x22;, text: &#x22;The describe service, exakit data-load or exakit connect. The helper calls these and does not reimplement them.&#x22;, code: &#x22;exakit describe AMAZON.ORDER_LINES&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The database&#x22;, text: &#x22;The Exasol database on this computer&#x22;, tone: &#x22;db&#x22; },
]"
/>

The rules the helpers follow:

* **The connection comes from the kit.** `nb.connect()` opens it from the kit's encrypted store. No helper prints or returns a host, a user or a password.
* **The kit does the work.** Describing a table is the kit's describe service. Loading is `exakit data-load`. Connecting a source is `exakit connect`.
* **SQL is shown.** `nb.sql` records each statement, `nb.show_sql()` prints the last one, and the workflow logs it.
* **Reads are live.** `nb.components()`, `nb.addons()`, `nb.connectors()` and the rest ask the kit when they are called.

Inside the guided view, `actions.py` lists every action as one or more lines of `exakit.nb` code. `actions.code(id, ...)` gives the exact cell text, and `actions.run(id, ...)` runs that text in the notebook's namespace and logs it. A screen changes nothing except through `actions.run`, which is why the **Code** view can always show what a card did.

The tests enforce a few more rules: every action calls something the helpers export, no screen names a dataset or a connector (the kit supplies those), no action shows a secret, and every helper has a page in these docs.

## The command reference [#the-command-reference]

The [command reference](/data-scientist/development/reference) lists every public helper of `exakit.nb`, 116 in all, with a one-line summary and a link to its page. The pages are generated from the docstrings in `exakit_nb`, one page per module.

From a notebook, the docs open at a command's page:

```python
import exakit.nb as nb
nb.docs(nb.describe)     # open one command's page
nb.docs("words")         # search the docs
```

The `exakit` commands are described in `setup/help/exakit.json`. `exakit <command> --help` shows a command's reference and changes nothing.

## Where things live [#where-things-live]

Everything is under the kit's home, `~/.exasol-starter-kit`, or `EXAKIT_HOME` when it is set. The main folders are:

| Path                     | What it holds                                                             |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `descriptors/`           | Approved column maps, one folder per table, every version kept            |
| `workflows/<id>.jsonl`   | Workflow logs                                                             |
| `bundles/<workflow id>/` | Hand-off bundles, each also as a zip                                      |
| `handoffs/`              | Training hand-offs for the ML Engineer                                    |
| `exakit.env`             | Settings such as the model's id and address                               |
| `credentials/`           | Secrets, readable by you only. Never read or print these from a notebook. |

The full table, including what an update touches and the schemas in the database, is in [Where things live](/data-scientist/development/where-things-live).

## Adding a command [#adding-a-command]

Four steps, and a test:

1. Add a function with a docstring to a module in `notebook/package/exakit_nb/`. Export it in `exakit_nb/__init__.py` and add its name to `__all__`.
2. Call it from the notebook it belongs to, guarded by a variable when it is optional.
3. Add one entry to `actions.ACTIONS` in `exakit_guide/actions.py`, so a card can have a button for it.
4. Regenerate the notebooks and the command reference with `python3 tools/notebooks.py --marimo` and `python3 tools/nb_docs.py`.

Then run `python3 -m unittest tests.test_notebook_guide tests.test_notebook_helpers tests.test_notebook_docs`. The full steps, with examples, are in [Add a command](/data-scientist/development/add-a-command).

## The notebooks [#the-notebooks]

The notebook sources are `notebook/notebooks/<persona>/<NN>_<name>.py`, in jupytext percent format. The `.ipynb` files and the Marimo versions are built from them:

```bash
python3 tools/notebooks.py --marimo            # rebuild
python3 tools/notebooks.py --check --marimo    # fail when a built file is stale
```

## Building these docs [#building-these-docs]

The documentation is MDX pages in `notebook/docs/content/docs/`, one folder per persona. The folder layout is the sidebar, and each folder's `meta.json` sets its title and page order.

```bash
npm install && npm run dev          # in notebook/docs: preview at http://localhost:3000/docs
npm run build                       # writes notebook/docs/out
python3 tools/nb_docs.py --publish  # copies it to notebook/docs/site, stamped with a digest
python3 tools/nb_docs.py --check    # fails when a generated page or the shipped site is stale
```

Users never need Node. The built site travels with the kit, and `nb.docs()` serves it from the kit's own Python, on this computer only. The full steps are in [These docs](/data-scientist/development/docs-site).

Everything under a persona's `reference/` folder is generated. Change the docstring and run `python3 tools/nb_docs.py`; do not edit the generated page.

## When the documentation does not open [#when-the-documentation-does-not-open]

`nb.docs()` reads the site from the kit copy. If it says the site is not there, run:

```python
nb.exakit("update", "notebook")
```

The site is served on this computer at one of the ports 8790 to 8809, the first one free. A port another program holds is skipped. When all of them are taken, any free port is used. To choose the port, set `EXAKIT_DOCS_PORT` before you start the notebooks.

If the notebook runs on another machine than your browser, the frame cannot reach the site. Run `nb.docs(browser=True)` on the machine that runs the kit.

To go back to the story, see [The data science workflow](/data-scientist).


# Where things live (/data-scientist/development/where-things-live)



Everything is under the kit's home, `~/.exasol-starter-kit` (or `EXAKIT_HOME` when set).

| Path                                         | What it holds                                                                |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `notebooks/starter-kit-notebooks/<persona>/` | Your copies of the notebooks                                                 |
| `notebooks/marimo/<persona>/`                | The Marimo versions                                                          |
| `descriptors/`                               | Approved column maps, one folder per table, every version kept               |
| `last-dataset`                               | The dataset approved last, which the notebooks follow                        |
| `workflows/<id>.jsonl`                       | Workflow logs                                                                |
| `last-workflow`                              | The workflow started or resumed last                                         |
| `bundles/<workflow id>/`                     | Hand-off bundles, each also as a zip                                         |
| `handoffs/`                                  | Training handoffs for the ML Engineer                                        |
| `exakit.env`                                 | Settings such as the model's id and address                                  |
| `credentials/`                               | Secrets, readable by you only. Never read or print these from a notebook.    |
| `kit/`                                       | The kit copy: scripts, datasets, the notebook package and this documentation |

## In the database [#in-the-database]

| Schema                                                 | What it holds                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `SEMANTIC_CATALOG`, `SEMANTIC_ADMIN`, `SEMANTIC_AGENT` | Exasol Semantic Views: the semantic models built from the approved column maps |
| `SEM_<MODEL>`                                          | A model's published semantic views, queried with Semantic SQL                  |
| `EXAKIT_PREPARED`                                      | Joined views and typed, cleaned views you chose to create                      |
| `VS_<NAME>`                                            | The tables of an external source named `<NAME>`                                |

## What an update touches [#what-an-update-touches]

* A kit notebook you did not edit is refreshed when the kit's version changes.
* A notebook you edited, or a file of your own, is never overwritten.
* A notebook you deleted is not copied back.
* Approved column maps, workflow logs and bundles are yours and are left alone.

## Further reading [#further-reading]

* [Virtual Schemas](https://docs.exasol.com/db/latest/database_concepts/virtual_schemas.htm), for the `VS_<NAME>` schemas.
* [Database users and roles](https://docs.exasol.com/db/latest/database_concepts/database_users_roles.htm), for the users behind the credentials folder.
* [exasol-labs/exasol-semantic-views](https://github.com/exasol-labs/exasol-semantic-views), for the `SEMANTIC_*` and `SEM_<MODEL>` schemas.
* [What the kit writes](/security/what-the-kit-writes) and [Credentials](/security/credentials), with the file modes and the limits of each.


# Your AI model in this stage (/data-scientist/model/ai-model)



## Your AI model in this stage [#your-ai-model-in-this-stage]

The AI model is optional. Every step in the model stage runs without one. Without a model, `nb.feature_ideas(lab)` still returns the rule-based ideas. With a model, `nb.feature_ideas(lab, ai=True)` adds up to four more.

Your model has one job here: it suggests feature ideas. It never sees rows, never approves a column map, and never runs SQL.

<Flow
  caption="An AI suggestion, from names to a tested idea"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;The kit sends names and roles&#x22;, text: &#x22;Column names, roles, the model scores so far, the five kinds it may use, and the target's name. Never a row or a value.&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Your model suggests up to four&#x22;, text: &#x22;Only of the five kinds below, each built from existing columns&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.feature_ideas(lab, ai=True, conn=connection)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;ai&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The kit checks each suggestion&#x22;, text: &#x22;Suggestions that name the target, or a column the data does not have, are dropped&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The kit tests the rest&#x22;, text: &#x22;Each one goes through the same verdict as any other idea&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.try_feature(lab, idea)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;You read the SQL and decide&#x22;, text: &#x22;No idea is kept without you&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
]"
/>

## What it is sent [#what-it-is-sent]

The code in `lab.py` builds one request with these parts:

* the target's name
* every column name and its role. A column marked sensitive is left out.
* the cross-validated score of each model so far, rounded to three decimals
* the five kinds of idea it may suggest
* a rule: suggest up to four, use only those kinds and existing column names, and never use the target or a column filled in after the outcome

No row and no value is sent.

## What it may suggest [#what-it-may-suggest]

Five kinds only. The kit builds each one as SQL and tests it like any other idea.

| Kind             | Columns                  | The SQL the kit writes                    |
| ---------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| `ratio_to_group` | a measure and a category | `"m" / AVG("m") OVER (PARTITION BY "c")`  |
| `combine`        | two categories           | `` `"a" \|\| ' · ' \|\| "b"` ``           |
| `days_since`     | a date                   | `DAYS_BETWEEN(CURRENT_DATE, "d")`         |
| `as_number`      | one column               | `CAST("c" AS DOUBLE)`                     |
| `is_missing`     | one column               | `CASE WHEN "c" IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END` |

A suggestion of another kind, or with the wrong number of columns, is dropped.

## What the kit checks, and what it cannot [#what-the-kit-checks-and-what-it-cannot]

The kit checks two things. It drops a suggestion that names the target, and a suggestion that names a column the data does not have. It reads up to four suggestions and no more.

The prompt also tells the model not to use a column written after the outcome. The kit cannot check that by itself. The verdict from `nb.try_feature` and your reading of the SQL are the check. An idea that scores above 0.98 on the held-out rows gets the verdict `suspicious`, and the kit tells you not to keep it.

## Where the data goes [#where-the-data-goes]

The model is the endpoint you set. It is called only when you pass `ai=True`, or when you run the themes step. With a model set up, feature ideas send names and roles, never rows.

The optional themes step in `01_explore` is different. It sends a sample of the newest texts on each side of the target to your model, so it needs a text column. The practice datasets have none, so the step skips.

## Tracing [#tracing]

When Langfuse is set up, each call is traced. Pass `conn=connection` to `nb.feature_ideas`, and the call goes into one trace named `feature-ideas`, tagged with the database session. Set-up is on [AI and Langfuse](/data-scientist/set-up/ai-and-langfuse).

## Set it up [#set-it-up]

Run `nb.model_setup()` in a notebook, or call `nb.use_model(MODEL_ID, PROVIDER_BASE_URL)` yourself. Without one, `nb.feature_ideas(lab, ai=True)` stops with the message "No AI model is set up". Check what is set with `nb.model_settings()`. The providers and where to find their keys are on [Set up Exasol](/data-scientist/set-up).

The model is never asked to approve anything, and it never changes your data.

Back to [Model](/data-scientist/model). Troubleshooting is on [Model: when it goes wrong](/data-scientist/model/troubleshooting).


# Start with a baseline (/data-scientist/model/baseline)



A model with every column is only worth keeping if it does better than a simple rule. The baseline is that simple rule. If a real model cannot beat it, the columns carry little signal about the outcome. The kit has two baselines.

## Start with a baseline [#start-with-a-baseline]

* **The notebook baseline** is a small logistic regression in `01_explore`. It uses three inputs: the category, the state and the month of the date.
* **The lab's baseline** is the model called `baseline` in each prediction task. For yes or no, it always gives the common answer. A constant prediction scores 0.5 ROC AUC, so any real model should score above 0.5.

<Flow
  caption="The notebook baseline, in 01_explore"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;Read the roles&#x22;, text: &#x22;The category, the entity and the date come from the approved column map&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Leave out the answer-givers&#x22;, text: &#x22;A flagged category or entity is skipped. The date is used only as its month.&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.leakage_check(connection, dataset)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Train on three quarters&#x22;, text: &#x22;A logistic regression, with one 0 or 1 column for each value&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Keep one quarter back&#x22;, text: &#x22;It is scored on the rows the model never saw. See Evaluate.&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/evaluate&#x22; },
]"
/>

## The notebook baseline [#the-notebook-baseline]

The cell reads the newest 20,000 rows when the table has a date, or the first 20,000 by key when it has none. The key makes a rerun read the same rows. The cell builds the features from the category, the state and the month, then trains this pipeline:

```python
model = Pipeline([
    ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")),
    ("classifier", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced")),
])
```

* `OneHotEncoder` turns each value of the category, the state and the month into a 0 or 1 column.
* `class_weight="balanced"` tells the model to weigh the rarer answer more, so it does not just predict the common one.
* The split is stratified, which keeps the same share of 1s on both sides, with a fixed seed (`random_state=0`). A quarter of the rows is kept back.

The cell prints how many rows it trained on and how many it kept back. It uses a category or an entity only when that column is not flagged by `nb.leakage_check`. The notebook's comment gives the reason for the check: a column written after the outcome "predicts the target perfectly on old rows and fails on new rows."

For `amazon_sales`, the baseline reads `CATEGORY`, `SHIP_STATE` and the month of `ORDER_DATE`. It never reads `STATUS`.

## Do not judge a rare answer by accuracy [#do-not-judge-a-rare-answer-by-accuracy]

When the answer is rare, accuracy is misleading. A model that always says "not fraud" is about 95% accurate on `fraud_transactions`, because 2,510 of its 51,000 rows are fraud (4.9%). `nb.data_checks` reports the rare answer and says what the always-common guess achieves. The readout note also compares every score with that guess. The reasons, and the metric the kit uses instead, are on the [rare answers](/data-scientist/evaluate/rare-answers) page of Evaluate.

## Where to go next [#where-to-go-next]

The lab trains many models on the same rows: [The model lab](/data-scientist/model/model-lab). Back to [Model](/data-scientist/model).


# Feature ideas (/data-scientist/model/feature-ideas)



## Feature ideas [#feature-ideas]

A feature idea is a new input for the model, made from columns you already have. The kit proposes them, writes the SQL that builds each one, and tests them. You decide which ones to keep. Nothing is kept by default.

<Flow
  caption="Trying one feature idea"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;The kit proposes ideas&#x22;, text: &#x22;Up to eight, each with the SQL that builds it&#x22;, code: &#x22;ideas = nb.feature_ideas(lab)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Retrain with the idea added&#x22;, text: &#x22;The picked model, on the same split, with the idea as one more input&#x22;, code: &#x22;tried = nb.try_feature(lab, ideas[0])&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Read the verdict&#x22;, text: &#x22;helps, same, hurts or suspicious, in plain words&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Keep it or leave it out&#x22;, text: &#x22;Keep an idea by passing its series to the next lab&#x22;, code: &#x22;features={idea.id: tried['series']}&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
]"
/>

## The ideas the kit makes [#the-ideas-the-kit-makes]

`nb.feature_ideas(lab)` makes these, when the data has the columns for them. It returns at most eight.

* **How long ago the date was**, when the table has a date. Newer and older records can behave differently.
* **A measure compared with its category's usual value**, for the first two measures and the first two categories.
* **Two categories together**, such as a category with a certain state.
* **A category column that holds numbers, read as a number**, when it has more than two values. The model can then learn that more is worse, or better.
* **Whether a measure is missing**, when more than 0.5% of its rows are blank.
* **Whether a long text mentions a problem**, for a text column with long values. The words are price, slow, crash, wrong, cancel and a few others in `NEGATIVE_WORDS`.

Each idea shows its title, the reason it was proposed, and the SQL. Read the SQL before you keep it. It is the same expression the kit would run on your table.

## Try an idea [#try-an-idea]

`nb.try_feature(lab, idea)` retrains the picked model with the idea added. It uses the same split and the same cross-validation folds, so the two scores can be compared. It returns a verdict and the idea's values as a series.

| Verdict      | When                                                                                             | What it means                                            |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `suspicious` | The held-out score is above 0.98 for yes or no, or above 0.995 for a number                      | The idea probably gives the answer away. Do not keep it. |
| `helps`      | Cross-validation rises by 0.005 or more, and the held-out score does not fall by more than 0.002 | Keep it, if you can explain why it should work.          |
| `hurts`      | Cross-validation falls by 0.005 or more                                                          | Leave it out.                                            |
| `same`       | Anything else                                                                                    | Not worth the extra column.                              |

These thresholds are the kit's rules of thumb. They are not statistical tests. A verdict of `helps` on a small held-out set can still be chance. Read the number of rows held out, and `cv_sd`, before you believe it.

## Keep an idea [#keep-an-idea]

To keep an idea, pass its series to the next lab with `features=`:

```python
kept_features = {}
kept_features[ideas[0].id] = tried["series"]          # only when the verdict is "helps"
lab = nb.model_lab(connection, dataset, "predict_yes_no", features=kept_features)
```

The notebook's `01_explore` does this for the first three ideas. It keeps the ones with the verdict `helps` and drops the others. A kept idea is used on the next run of the lab cell.

Back to [Model](/data-scientist/model). The AI model's part in feature ideas is on [Your AI model in this stage](/data-scientist/model/ai-model).


# Model (/data-scientist/model)



Modelling turns the columns you approved into a prediction: will this order be cancelled, is this payment fraud, which rows look unusual. A model is only useful if it beats a simple guess, so start with the simplest one and improve it step by step. The kit gives you a baseline model in `01_explore`, a model lab that trains several models on the same rows, and feature ideas that you test before you keep them. Everything trains on this computer with scikit-learn, the Python machine-learning library the kit includes.

## The flow [#the-flow]

<Flow
  caption="From approved roles to a model you can judge"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;You approve the roles&#x22;, text: &#x22;The target and the groups come from the column map&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/explore&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Train the baseline&#x22;, text: &#x22;A small logistic regression, with the answer-givers left out&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.leakage_check(connection, dataset)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/model/baseline&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Run the model lab&#x22;, text: &#x22;Every model of one task trains on the same rows&#x22;, code: 'nb.model_lab(connection, dataset, &#x22;predict_yes_no&#x22;)', tone: &#x22;kit&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/model/model-lab&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Try feature ideas (optional)&#x22;, text: &#x22;Each idea is retrained on the same split before you keep it&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.try_feature(lab, ideas[0])&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/model/feature-ideas&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;You decide what to keep&#x22;, text: &#x22;A verdict says whether an idea helped. Scoring on unseen rows is in Evaluate.&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/evaluate&#x22; },
]"
/>

## Where you do it [#where-you-do-it]

| Guided view                                                                                                 | Notebook code                                                                          | Terminal                             |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `01_explore`: the **Build a model** card runs the model lab. The baseline's result is in the same notebook. | The cells **Train a baseline model** and **The model lab (optional)** in `01_explore`. | None. Training runs in the notebook. |

The first cell of `01_explore` holds the settings. `DATASET` picks the data. `USE_PREPARED = True` makes the model read the typed, cleaned view that [Prepare](/data-scientist/prepare) creates. The lab cell looks like this:

```python
LAB_TASK = "predict_yes_no"   # or "predict_number", "find_groups", "find_unusual"
lab_data = nb.lab_data(connection, dataset)   # read once; lab_data.left_out says what was left out and why
kept_features = {}
lab = nb.model_lab(connection, dataset, LAB_TASK, model="all", target_number=None, data=lab_data, features=kept_features)
```

## How we used it [#how-we-used-it]

The sample dataset `amazon_sales` is the table `AMAZON.ORDER_LINES`. It has 128,975 order lines. 18,332 of them (14.2%) are cancelled, which is the target `CANCELLED`.

* **The baseline** uses three inputs only: the category, the state and the month of `ORDER_DATE`. It does not read `STATUS`, which gives the target away. See [Start with a baseline](/data-scientist/model/baseline).
* **The lab** scores with ROC AUC, because the rarer answer is above 5%. It splits by time, so it learns from the older rows and is tested on the newer ones. See [The model lab](/data-scientist/model/model-lab).

The messy dataset, `fraud_transactions`, has a rare answer, no date and placeholder values. Its differences are listed in [The model lab](/data-scientist/model/model-lab).

## In this stage [#in-this-stage]

<Cards>
  <Card title="Start with a baseline" href="/data-scientist/model/baseline" description="The simplest model, and the score a real model must beat" />

  <Card title="The model lab" href="/data-scientist/model/model-lab" description="What the lab reads, how it splits the rows, and what it leaves out" />

  <Card title="The models the lab tries" href="/data-scientist/model/the-models" description="Every model, the rule that picks one, and the settings" />

  <Card title="Feature ideas" href="/data-scientist/model/feature-ideas" description="New inputs built from your columns, and the verdict for each" />

  <Card title="Your AI model in this stage" href="/data-scientist/model/ai-model" description="What an AI model may suggest here, and what it is sent" />

  <Card title="Saving, MLflow and training in the database" href="/data-scientist/model/saving-and-mlflow" description="What is kept after a run, and where the in-database path starts" />

  <Card title="When it goes wrong" href="/data-scientist/model/troubleshooting" description="The warnings and errors you see while you model" />
</Cards>

## What you have at the end [#what-you-have-at-the-end]

A baseline score, the lab's leaderboard with the model it picked, the importance list, and the feature ideas you kept with their verdicts. The next step is to check the score on rows the model never trained on, in [Evaluate](/data-scientist/evaluate).

<StageNav n="5" />


# The model lab (/data-scientist/model/model-lab)



`nb.model_lab` trains one task on your approved data. It trains every model of that task on the same rows, scores each one, and picks the best. It is the second half of the model stage, after the baseline. The lab uses the same approved column map as the notebook baseline, but it reads more columns and more rows.

## The tasks [#the-tasks]

| Task                | What it learns                         | Example                           |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Predict yes or no   | The 0/1 target                         | Will this order be cancelled?     |
| Predict a number    | A number you name with `target_number` | What will this order's amount be? |
| Find natural groups | Nothing: no outcome is needed          | Which orders look alike?          |
| Find unusual rows   | Nothing: no outcome is needed          | Which rows sit far from the rest? |

<Flow
  caption="What the lab does with your approved data"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;Read the approved columns&#x22;, text: &#x22;Every column with a role, up to 50,000 rows&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.lab_data(connection, dataset)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Leave out what it must not read&#x22;, text: &#x22;Answer-givers, personal data, keys, identifiers and free text&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Split the rows&#x22;, text: &#x22;The newest rows by time, a random share, or whole groups&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/evaluate/hold-out&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Train every model of the task&#x22;, text: &#x22;On the same training rows, with cross-validation&#x22;, code: 'nb.model_lab(connection, dataset, &#x22;predict_yes_no&#x22;)', tone: &#x22;kit&#x22;, href: &#x22;/data-scientist/model/the-models&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;Score on the held-out rows&#x22;, text: &#x22;The held-out rows are scored, not used to choose&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
]"
/>

## What the lab reads [#what-the-lab-reads]

The kit decides the inputs from the roles in the column map. You do not type column names. The table gives each role's treatment.

| Role                | How the lab uses it                     | Left out when                                       |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `measure`           | As a number                             | It gives the answer away, or is personal data       |
| `category`, `flag`  | As groups: one 0 or 1 column per value  | It gives the answer away, or is personal data       |
| `time`              | Only the month of the date              | Never left out, but the full date is not used       |
| `key`, `identifier` | Not used as inputs                      | Almost every row is different                       |
| `text`              | Not used, except through a feature idea | Always. Free text is not a column the lab can read. |
| `other`             | Not used                                | Always: its role says leave it out                  |
| target              | The answer the model learns             | It is never an input                                |

The lab reads at most 50,000 rows (`ROW_LIMIT` in the code). When the table has a date, those are the newest rows. Otherwise the query sorts by its first column and keeps 50,000 rows.

## What the lab leaves out, and why [#what-the-lab-leaves-out-and-why]

`lab_data.left_out` lists every column the lab did not use, with its reason. Read it after every run. The reasons come from the code in `lab.py`:

* **gives the answer away**: the column is in the list from `nb.leakage_check`. See [Leakage](/data-scientist/evaluate/leakage) on the Evaluate pages.
* **personal data**: the column is marked sensitive in the column map. It is never used as an input.
* **different for (almost) every row, so there is nothing general to learn**: a key or an identifier.
* **free text: see the feature ideas**: a text column.
* **marked Leave out**: the column's role is `other`.

```python
lab_data = nb.lab_data(connection, dataset)
print(lab_data.left_out)   # every column left out, and why
```

## The metric and the split for amazon_sales [#the-metric-and-the-split-for-amazon_sales]

* **The metric.** The rarer answer is 14.2% of rows, which is above 5%, so the lab scores with ROC AUC. Below 5%, it uses PR AUC instead. Both are explained on [Reading ROC AUC](/data-scientist/evaluate/roc-auc) and [Metrics](/data-scientist/evaluate/metrics).
* **The rows.** `amazon_sales` has 128,975 rows, so the lab reads the newest 50,000 by `ORDER_DATE`.
* **The split.** `ORDER_DATE` is a date, so the lab uses a time split. It learns from the oldest 75% of those rows and is tested on the newest 25%.
* **The inputs.** Every measure, category and flag column the column map gives a role to, plus the month of the date. Keys, identifiers, text, personal data and the answer-givers are left out.

<Callout>
  Check `AMOUNT` before you trust the lab. The dataset README says `AMOUNT` and `QTY` change once an order is cancelled, so a model that reads them learns the answer it was given. The leakage check tests only columns with 2 to 50 distinct values (`GROUPABLE` in `data_checks.py`), so it may not flag `AMOUNT`. To see how many values it has, run `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT "AMOUNT") FROM AMAZON.ORDER_LINES`. If `AMOUNT` tops `lab.importance`, leave it out yourself:

  ```python
  leaks = nb.leakage_check(connection, dataset) + ["AMOUNT"]
  lab = nb.model_lab(connection, dataset, "predict_yes_no", leaks=leaks)
  ```
</Callout>

## What the model leans on [#what-the-model-leans-on]

`lab.importance` lists up to eight inputs, the strongest first. For each input, the kit scrambles its values on the held-out rows and measures how far the score drops. A large drop means the model relies on that input. Only inputs whose drop is above zero are listed.

The list is a lead, not proof. A value with few rows can look strong by chance.

## The messy dataset: fraud_transactions [#the-messy-dataset-fraud_transactions]

The README of `fraud_transactions` gives 51,000 rows, with 4.9% of them fraud. Measured on the database, the table has 50,000 distinct `TRANSACTION_ID` values, so 1,000 ids appear twice. Three things change for the lab:

* **A rare answer.** Under 5% of rows are 1s, so the lab scores with PR AUC, which focuses on finding the rare rows. The lab records the reason in `lab.run.notes`: "The 1s are rare, so the score is PR AUC, which focuses on finding them."
* **No date.** The table has only the hour of the day. The lab splits at random, stratified so both sides keep the same share of fraud. With no date it sorts by the first column of its query and keeps 50,000 of the 51,000 rows. The notebook baseline reads the first 20,000 rows by `ROW_ID` and leaves the month out.
* **Placeholder values.** The README lists 1,530 `Unknown Device` and 1,530 `Invalid Method` values. The lab does not clean them. Each placeholder becomes one more category value. To read the typed, cleaned view from [Prepare](/data-scientist/prepare) instead, set `USE_PREPARED = True` in `01_explore`.

## Settings [#settings]

Pass settings by name. An unknown name is an error.

| Setting                                                     | What it does                                                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `train_pct`                                                 | The share of rows used for training, from 50 to 90. The default is 75.                           |
| `split_method`                                              | `time`, `random` or `group`. See [Hold-out](/data-scientist/evaluate/hold-out).                  |
| `split_group`                                               | The column whose whole groups are kept on one side, for `group`                                  |
| `folds`                                                     | The number of cross-validation folds on the training rows. The default is 5.                     |
| `effort`                                                    | `fast`, `balanced` (the default) or `thorough`. It sets the number of trees: 100, 200 or 400.    |
| `max_depth`, `C`, `neighbours`, `learning_rate`, `clusters` | The settings of the models that use them                                                         |
| `contamination`                                             | The share of rows to flag as unusual. The default is 2%. The code keeps it between 0.5% and 20%. |

The full signatures are in the [model lab reference](/data-scientist/development/reference/lab).

Back to [Model](/data-scientist/model). Next: [The models the lab tries](/data-scientist/model/the-models).


# Saving, MLflow and training in the database (/data-scientist/model/saving-and-mlflow)



Three things sit beside the model lab and are easy to confuse: keeping a result, the optional MLflow record, and the training that runs inside the database. The Data Scientist notebooks use the first only. The other two belong to the ML Engineer's path.

## Saving a model [#saving-a-model]

Nothing in the Data Scientist notebooks saves a fitted model to disk or to the database. The lab's fitted model lives in your kernel until you stop it. To keep a result, keep the numbers: the board, the importance list and the notes.

The workflow log records only that a model ran, with its task, its row count and, for the small model, its score. See [The workflow log](/data-scientist/monitor/the-workflow-log).

## MLflow, when it is installed [#mlflow-when-it-is-installed]

MLflow is an optional record of training runs. The Data Scientist notebooks do not start MLflow runs. The runs come from the in-database training that the ML Engineer's notebooks do, described below.

* `nb.use_mlflow()` sets where runs are recorded for this kernel. An empty address means the kit's own MLflow server (`exakit mlflow start`), or whatever the shell set. `nb.use_mlflow(login=True)` asks for a username and a password in a hidden box.
* `nb.check_mlflow()` checks the client and the server. If the client is missing, it says to run `exakit update notebook`.
* `exakit mlflow start` installs the MLflow server into the notebook environment when it is missing.

The settings are listed in [Model, Langfuse and MLflow settings](/data-scientist/development/reference/setup-env).

## Training inside the database (the ML Engineer's path) [#training-inside-the-database-the-ml-engineers-path]

This is not a Data Scientist step, but it is where the kit's trained models come from. `nb.prepare_training(conn, ds, handoff, container=..., seed=0)` prepares in-database training from a training hand-off:

* It refuses a hand-off that is stale, and a random split that nobody asked for. See [The training hand-off](/data-scientist/communicate/training-hand-off) for what a hand-off holds.
* It creates a feature view in `STARTER_KIT`, drops features that are constant, and writes a training function that fits a logistic regression with a fixed seed.
* It returns a plan. The caller runs `plan.create_script`, then `plan.training_sql`.

It needs a Python container inside the database: `PYTHON3_ML` (`exakit udf-use default`) or `PYTHON3` (`exakit udf-setup`). Both come from the udf-devkit add-on, `exakit marketplace udf-devkit`. The [add-ons page](/kit/tools/add-ons) explains how add-ons are installed.

Back to [Model](/data-scientist/model).


# The models the lab tries (/data-scientist/model/the-models)



The lab does not rely on one model. For each task it trains every model in a list on the same training rows, and it picks one. This page lists the models, the rule for the pick, and how to choose a model yourself. Every model is from scikit-learn. The key in brackets is the name you pass as `model=`.

## The models the lab tries [#the-models-the-lab-tries]

| Task             | Models                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | How the best one is picked                                                                         |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `predict_yes_no` | baseline (`baseline`), logistic regression (`logistic`), logistic regression with L1 (`logistic_l1`), decision tree (`decision_tree`), random forest (`random_forest`), extra trees (`extra_trees`), gradient boosting (`boosting`), k-nearest neighbours (`knn`), naive Bayes (`naive_bayes`), linear support vector machine (`svm`) | Cross-validated ROC AUC, or PR AUC when the rarer answer is under 5%                               |
| `predict_number` | baseline (`baseline`), linear (`linear`), ridge (`ridge`), lasso (`lasso`), decision tree, random forest, extra trees, gradient boosting, k-nearest neighbours                                                                                                                                                                        | Cross-validated R squared                                                                          |
| `find_groups`    | k-means (`kmeans`), Gaussian mixture (`gaussian_mixture`), hierarchical (`agglomerative`)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | Silhouette score. If you do not set the number of groups, the lab tries 2 to 6 and keeps the best. |
| `find_unusual`   | isolation forest (`isolation_forest`), local outlier factor (`lof`)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | No score. The share you set as `contamination` (2% by default) decides how many rows are flagged.  |

## How the best one is picked [#how-the-best-one-is-picked]

With `model="all"`, the lab does this:

1. It scores each model by cross-validation on the training rows. The score is the metric for the task.
2. It takes the model with the highest mean score.
3. It goes down a list of models from simplest to most complex. The first model on that list whose score is within 0.01 of the best wins.

The order is: logistic regression, linear, ridge, logistic L1, lasso, naive Bayes, decision tree, k-nearest neighbours, SVM, random forest, extra trees, gradient boosting. The baseline is not on that list. It is picked only when it has the highest score and no model on the list is within 0.01 of it.

The pick is made on cross-validation. The held-out rows are scored after the pick, for reading. They do not choose the model.

<Callout>
  The 0.01 rule is a rule for choosing a simple model. It is not a test that the gap between two models is real. To judge a gap, read `cv_sd` on the board. See [Comparing models](/data-scientist/evaluate/comparing-models) on the Evaluate pages.
</Callout>

## Choose a model yourself [#choose-a-model-yourself]

Pass one key to `model=`, and the lab trains that model and its baseline on the same rows:

```python
lab = nb.model_lab(connection, dataset, "predict_yes_no", model="logistic")
```

With a named model, the pick is yours: the result's `chosen_by` is `you`, and the board holds only that model and the baseline.

## The settings that change the models [#the-settings-that-change-the-models]

`effort` sets the number of trees for the tree models: `fast` 100, `balanced` 200 (the default) and `thorough` 400. The other settings are listed on [The model lab](/data-scientist/model/model-lab#settings). Back to [Model](/data-scientist/model).


# Troubleshooting (/data-scientist/model/troubleshooting)



Each entry quotes the message the kit prints, or describes the step that stops.

<Accordions type="multiple">
  <Accordion title="A model step is skipped">
    The dataset has no target, or no category or entity that is free of the answer, so the baseline cannot run. The step says so. Choose a target in the column map, approve it, and run the notebook again. `nb.model_settings()` shows whether the AI steps have a model. No model is needed for the baseline or the lab.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="The model lab says nothing to predict was chosen">
    The lab was asked to predict yes or no, but the column map has no yes-or-no target. The error reads "Nothing to predict was chosen". Pick a 0 or 1 column as the target in the column map, or choose another task: predict a number, find natural groups or find unusual rows.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="One side of the split has only one answer">
    The error reads "One side of the split has only one answer, so no score can be computed". A time split can put all the 1s on one side. Change the split to `split_method="random"`, which is stratified for yes or no. See [Hold-out](/data-scientist/evaluate/hold-out).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Only a few rows with a 1 are held out">
    The warning reads "Only N rows with a 1 are held out, so the held-out score is shaky". It appears when fewer than 30 rows with a 1 are held out. Lower `train_pct` (50 is the lowest it accepts), so more rows are held out.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="No model could be trained on this data">
    The error reads "No model could be trained on this data", and lists the reason for each model that failed. The most common cause is a dataset with almost no rows on one side of the answer. Check the split first.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="No AI model is set up">
    `nb.feature_ideas(lab, ai=True)` stops with "No AI model is set up". Run `nb.model_setup()`, or `nb.use_model(MODEL_ID, PROVIDER_BASE_URL)`. Or call `nb.feature_ideas(lab)` without `ai=True`, which needs no model.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="The lab leaves out a column you expected it to use">
    Read `lab_data.left_out`. It gives the reason for each column left out: gives the answer away, personal data, a key or identifier, free text, or marked Leave out. A column marked sensitive, or flagged by the leakage check, is not used. Change the column map if the role is wrong, and approve it again.
  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

Back to [Model](/data-scientist/model).


# External sources (/data-scientist/get-the-data/external-sources)



An external source is a database or a lake somewhere else. The kit reads it where it lives. Nothing is copied. The kit connects it as a **virtual schema**, which is a schema in your local database whose tables point at the source. A query fetches the rows it needs at the moment you run it.

The kit connects through its source engine, the same engine `exakit connect` runs.

## The kinds the kit can connect [#the-kinds-the-kit-can-connect]

* PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and MongoDB.
* Iceberg and Delta tables through a lakehouse catalog: Iceberg REST, Unity Catalog or AWS Glue.
* A folder of Parquet files, or document files in S3 or Azure Blob Storage.

These helpers list the kinds and what each one asks:

```python
nb.connectors()                        # every kind the kit can connect
nb.connector_inputs("postgresql")      # what that kind asks, with the required inputs marked
nb.connected_sources(connection)       # the sources connected now, with their table counts
nb.load_source(connection, None)       # lists the connected sources, and loads nothing
```

## Connect from this computer [#connect-from-this-computer]

The database runs in its own virtual machine. On macOS, the database cannot reach this computer as `localhost`.

* Use `192.168.64.1` for a database on this computer. If you give `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` on macOS, the kit replaces it with that address and prints one line about it. The source must then listen on that address too, not only on the loopback address.
* For a cloud source, allow this computer's public IP address at the source. The card shows the address. `exakit connect` shows it as its first line on a terminal.

## A lakehouse [#a-lakehouse]

A lakehouse is one connector for several things. It has two settings: a catalog, and where its files are. Each combination asks for different details. In the **Data source** list it appears as a tree. Pick a leaf and both settings are chosen. Pick the lakehouse itself and the settings are asked one at a time.

```python
form = nb.connector_inputs("lakehouse")
form["tree"]                                                       # the picks, as the tree shows them
form = nb.connector_inputs("lakehouse", catalog="unity", files="s3")
form["inputs"]                                                     # what that combination asks
nb.connect_source("lakehouse", "lake", catalog="unity", files="s3", workspace_url="https://...", namespace="main.sales")
```

Some combinations have two secrets: the catalog login and the storage keys. The catalog login is asked like any password. The storage keys go to the kit in a file only you can read, and the file is removed as soon as the kit has read it.

## An example: a PostgreSQL source [#an-example-a-postgresql-source]

This example reads a PostgreSQL database that runs on this computer. Your connector, host, database and table will differ.

```python
CONNECTOR = "postgresql"
SOURCE_NAME = "sales"                                   # its tables appear as VS_SALES
SOURCE_URL = "postgres://reader@192.168.64.1:5432/shop" # the password is asked in a hidden box
source_reading = nb.read_connection_string(CONNECTOR, SOURCE_URL)
source_test = nb.test_source(CONNECTOR, SOURCE_NAME, url=SOURCE_URL)
connected = nb.connect_source(CONNECTOR, SOURCE_NAME, url=SOURCE_URL)
SOURCE = None                                           # or "VS_SALES.ORDERS"
source_data = nb.load_source(connection, SOURCE or connected)
```

Run the cells in order. The reading shows what the connection string did not give. The test checks the inputs and whether this computer reaches the host and port. It changes nothing. The connect step runs the kit's connect command and makes the virtual schema.

## Step by step: a new external source [#step-by-step-a-new-external-source]

The **Choose your data** card walks through a new connection one step at a time. Each step asks one question. The steps you see depend on the source you pick.

<Steps>
  <Step>
    ### Connection [#connection]

    Pick a connection you already have, or **New connection…**. Your existing connections are listed with their table counts. Choose one and press **Use this data** to load a table from it.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Data source [#data-source]

    Pick the kind of source: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, MongoDB, a lakehouse, or a file in S3 or Azure Blob Storage. Each kind has the same questions as `exakit connect`. A card shows the kit's own names for them.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Settings [#settings]

    Shown only for a source with several kinds in one. A lakehouse asks for its catalog and where its files are, then asks only what that combination needs. See the lakehouse section above.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Connection string or manual [#connection-string-or-manual]

    Paste a connection string and press **Next**, and the kit reads it. The steps after it ask only for what the string did not give. Or choose **Manual configuration** and type each detail.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Name [#name]

    A lower-case name, for example `sales`. Its tables appear as `VS_SALES`.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Details [#details]

    The inputs the kit still needs: the host, the database, the user and the password. The password goes into a hidden box. It is never shown, saved or logged by the card.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Optional settings [#optional-settings]

    A port, a CA certificate file or another optional value. The kit fills in its own default for each one you leave alone.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Test connection, then Connect and use this data [#test-connection-then-connect-and-use-this-data]

    **Test connection** checks the inputs and whether this computer reaches the source. It changes nothing and needs no password. **Connect and use this data** runs the kit's connect command with the password on its standard input, then loads the table you chose.
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Flow
  caption="A new external source, step by step"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;You name the source&#x22;, text: &#x22;The kind, a connection string or the details, and a name&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The kit checks the inputs&#x22;, text: &#x22;Every input, the way the kit's connect form checks it&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.test_source(...)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;This computer reaches the source&#x22;, text: &#x22;The host and port answer from here&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;You enter the password&#x22;, text: &#x22;In a hidden box. It goes to the kit only.&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The kit connects&#x22;, text: &#x22;A connection is saved and a virtual schema is made&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.connect_source(...)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The tables read live&#x22;, text: &#x22;VS_SALES.ORDERS is read from the source when you query it&#x22;, tone: &#x22;db&#x22; },
]"
/>

## Passwords [#passwords]

* A password is asked in a hidden box. The kit receives it on its standard input.
* It is never written into a cell, the code view, a command line or the workflow log.
* A password inside a connection string is used and never shown.
* In Marimo there is no hidden box. Pass a password field, `mo.ui.text(kind="password")`, as the `password` argument, or pass a `password_file`.

## Live sources and AI [#live-sources-and-ai]

A table from an external source is read from the source as you query it. Before sampled rows from a live source go to a model, the notebook names the source and asks. Only a yes sends them. A table in the database does not ask.

Back to [Get the data](/data-scientist/get-the-data). Next: [The data map](/data-scientist/get-the-data/the-data-map).


# Get the data (/data-scientist/get-the-data)



Every data project starts with data that is in one place, can be read again, and is the same each time you read it. In this stage you put a table in front of the kit. The kit offers three origins: a sample dataset that comes with the kit, your own file or folder, and an external database or lake that the kit reads live. Each origin ends in a table the rest of the workflow can describe.

<Flow
  caption="Choosing an origin, loading it and reading it in the data map"
  steps="[
  { title: &#x22;You pick an origin&#x22;, text: &#x22;A kit dataset, your own file or folder, a table already in the database, or an external source&#x22;, tone: &#x22;you&#x22;, href: &#x22;/kit/data/load-data&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The kit loads it&#x22;, text: &#x22;A sample or your file is copied into a table. An external source is connected, not copied.&#x22;, code: &#x22;exakit data-load amazon_sales&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The table is in the database&#x22;, text: &#x22;AMAZON.ORDER_LINES, MY_DATA.ORDERS or VS_SALES.ORDERS&#x22;, tone: &#x22;db&#x22; },
  { title: &#x22;The data map lists it&#x22;, text: &#x22;Every table by origin, with its rows, its column map and its links&#x22;, code: &#x22;nb.data_map(connection)&#x22;, tone: &#x22;kit&#x22; },
]"
/>

The flow is the same for all three origins. Only the first loading step differs. A sample dataset loads once and stays. Your file is copied into a table. An external source stays where it is: the kit creates a **virtual schema**, a schema in your local database whose tables point at a database or lake somewhere else. Its name is `VS_<NAME>`, where `<NAME>` is the name you gave the connection. Its tables are read when you query them.

You do not need a terminal for this stage. Every step runs from a cell or a card. The terminal commands are listed for scripts and for people who prefer them.

## Where you do it [#where-you-do-it]

| Guided view                                                                                                | Notebook code                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Terminal                                                                                           |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The **Choose your data** card in `00_quickstart`. Pick a kit dataset, your own data or an external source. | The shared cells in `00_quickstart`, under *Choose a dataset*, *Load your own data*, *An external source*: `SAMPLE`, `MY_DATA`, `MY_SCHEMA`, `MY_TABLE`, `CONNECTOR`, `SOURCE_URL`, `SOURCE`, then `nb.first(...)`, which picks the first loaded source | `exakit data-load` for a kit dataset, a file or a folder. `exakit connect` for an external source. |

## In this stage [#in-this-stage]

<Cards>
  <Card title="Sample datasets" href="/data-scientist/get-the-data/sample-datasets" description="amazon_sales and fraud_transactions: what is in each, with the numbers" />

  <Card title="Your own file" href="/data-scientist/get-the-data/your-own-files" description="Load a CSV, Parquet, JSON or Excel file, a folder, or a table already in the database" />

  <Card title="External sources" href="/data-scientist/get-the-data/external-sources" description="Connect a database or lake that stays where it is, step by step, and handle passwords" />

  <Card title="The data map" href="/data-scientist/get-the-data/the-data-map" description="Every table by origin, its column map state and its links" />

  <Card title="The dataset" href="/data-scientist/get-the-data/the-dataset" description="A table with its approved column map, and how a notebook picks one" />

  <Card title="Troubleshooting" href="/data-scientist/get-the-data/troubleshooting" description="File, source and table problems" />
</Cards>

## What you have at the end [#what-you-have-at-the-end]

A table that the kit can describe, chosen by `nb.first(...)` as `chosen_data`, and a data map that shows it. The table has no approved column map yet. The next stage reviews the roles and approves them.

Next: [Explore and understand](/data-scientist/explore).

<StageNav n="2" />


# Sample datasets (/data-scientist/get-the-data/sample-datasets)



The kit ships two sample datasets, so you can run every stage before you bring your own data. `amazon_sales` is a clean table of orders. `fraud_transactions` has repeats, gaps and placeholders on purpose, so the cleaning steps have something to find. Both load with the same cell.

## Load one [#load-one]

The first cell of `00_quickstart` picks the dataset:

```python
SAMPLE = "amazon_sales"   # or "fraud_transactions", or None
sample_data = nb.load_sample(connection, SAMPLE)
```

If the dataset is not in the database, the cell runs `exakit data-load amazon_sales` and waits for it. If it is already there, the cell says it is loaded and uses it. `nb.sample_datasets()` lists the kit's datasets and which are loaded.

## How we used it: amazon_sales [#how-we-used-it-amazon_sales]

The table is `AMAZON.ORDER_LINES`. It holds order lines of one fashion seller. Each row is one line of an order, so the key is `ORDER_LINE_ID`, and the time column is `ORDER_DATE`. The target for the worked examples is `CANCELLED`, which is 1 when the line was cancelled.

These numbers come from a real local database, read with read-only queries on 12 November 2026:

```sh
exakit sql 'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AMAZON.ORDER_LINES'
exakit sql 'SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT ORDER_ID) FROM AMAZON.ORDER_LINES'
exakit sql 'SELECT MIN(ORDER_DATE), MAX(ORDER_DATE) FROM AMAZON.ORDER_LINES'
exakit sql 'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AMAZON.ORDER_LINES WHERE CANCELLED = 1'
```

| Query                           | Result                          |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `COUNT(*)`                      | 128,975 rows                    |
