# Model lab (/data-scientist/development/reference/lab)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

```python
lab = nb.model_lab(connection, dataset, "predict_yes_no")            # every model of the task, same split
lab = nb.model_lab(connection, dataset, "find_groups", clusters=4)   # or one task's settings by name
lab.board, lab.pick, lab.importance, lab.note                        # what came out
ideas = nb.feature_ideas(lab); nb.try_feature(lab, ideas[0])        # a feature idea, tried on the same split
```

Tasks
predict_yes_no   classification (supervised): the approved 0/1 target
predict_number   regression (supervised): a number column the user picks
find_groups      clustering (unsupervised): no target
find_unusual     anomaly detection (unsupervised): no target

Models are scikit-learn only (already in the kit). "Compare all" trains every
model of the task on identical rows and picks the best cross-validated score,
preferring the simpler model within 0.01. A single model can also be chosen.

The split is the user's: 50-90% for training, by time (newest held out), random
(stratified for yes/no) or by group (one group never on both sides), with 3, 5
or 10 cross-validation folds on the training side. Held-out rows are scored once.

## nb.feature_ideas [#feature_ideas]

```python
nb.feature_ideas(lab: Lab, *, ai: bool=False, conn=None) -> list[Idea]
```

Feature ideas for this lab's data, each with the SQL that would make it: try one with try_feature. With
`ai`, your AI model (nb.use_model) adds up to four more, of kinds the lab can build and test; it is sent the
column names, their roles and the scores - never a row or a value - and the call is traced when Langfuse is on
(`conn` tags the trace with the database session).

**Used in:** `data-scientist/01_explore`

## nb.Lab [#Lab]

```python
class nb.Lab
```

One model-lab run: the task, its settings, the data it read and what came out (board and pick for a
prediction, groups or unusual rows otherwise). `features` are the feature ideas it was trained with.

| Member          | What it is             |
| --------------- | ---------------------- |
| `task`          | `str`                  |
| `model`         | `str`                  |
| `settings`      | `dict`                 |
| `data`          | `Data`                 |
| `run`           | `Run`                  |
| `result`        | `dict`                 |
| `target_number` | \`str                  | None\` |
| `features`      | `dict[str, pd.Series]` |
| `note`          | `str`                  |
| `dataset`       | `object`               |
| `board`         |                        |
| `pick`          |                        |
| `importance`    |                        |

## nb.lab_data [#lab_data]

```python
nb.lab_data(conn, ds, leaks: list[str] | None=None) -> Data
```

The approved data the lab trains on, read once (newest first, at most ROW_LIMIT rows): every usable column,
with the ones that give the answer away (nb.leakage_check, unless `leaks` is given) and personal data left out
(`.left_out` says why). Pass it to model_lab(data=...) to train several times without reading it again.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/01_explore`

## nb.model_lab [#model_lab]

```python
nb.model_lab(
    conn,
    ds,
    task: str='predict_yes_no',
    *,
    model: str='all',
    target_number: str | None=None,
    leaks: list[str] | None=None,
    features: dict[str, pd.Series] | None=None,
    data: Data | None=None,
    **settings,
) -> Lab
```

Train `task` on the approved dataset: `predict_yes_no` (its target), `predict_number` (`target_number`),
`find_groups` or `find_unusual`. `model` is one model's key or "all" (each of the task, same rows, the
simpler one picked within 0.01). `settings` by name: train_pct, split_method (time, random, group),
split_group, folds, effort, max_depth, C, neighbours, learning_rate, clusters, contamination. Columns that give
the answer away (nb.leakage_check, unless `leaks` is given) and personal data are left out.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/01_explore`

## nb.try_feature [#try_feature]

```python
nb.try_feature(lab: Lab, idea: Idea) -> dict
```

Retrain the lab's picked model with `idea` added, on the same split: \{verdict, text, series}. Keep it by
passing features=\{idea.id: result\["series"]} to the next model_lab.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/01_explore`


# In-database training (/data-scientist/development/reference/ml-train)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

```python
CONTAINER = nb.ml_train.udf_container()                        # the container alias training runs on (PYTHON3_ML, else PYTHON3)
handoff = nb.ml_train.training_handoff(conn, ds)               # explore's file (stale: refused), else built from the descriptor
plan = nb.prepare_training(conn, ds, handoff, container=CONTAINER, seed=0)   # refuses a stale handoff or an unasked-for random split
conn.execute(plan.create_script); run.execute(plan.training_sql)
path = nb.ml_train.export_coefficients(run, handoff)           # <id>-v<n>.coefficients.json beside the handoff
```

Determinism (AC-ML3.4): the plan is a pure function of the handoff and the options - the features keep the handoff's
order (the input schema, which the feature view fixes), a constant feature is dropped by a MIN/MAX query whose answer
depends on the data alone, and the rendered UDF trains `LogisticRegression(random_state=seed, solver="lbfgs")` over
rows it sorts first - so the same handoff, seed and data give the same metrics and the same coefficients.

## nb.prepare_training [#prepare_training]

```python
nb.prepare_training(
    conn,
    ds: Dataset,
    handoff: dict[str, Any],
    *,
    schema: str='EXASOL_MLFLOW',
    name: str='TRAIN_FROM_HANDOFF',
    container: str | None=None,
    seed: int=0,
    C: float=1.0,
    max_iter: int=1000,
    model_dir: str | None=None,
    class_weight: str | None=None,
) -> TrainingPlan
```

Refuse stale input, create the view, drop constant features and render the UDF and training SELECT.

The caller creates `create_script` then passes `training_sql` to exasol_mlflow\.start_run().
`container` is the alias of the Python container the UDF runs on (the notebook's CONTAINER); None resolves it
with udf_container() - PYTHON3_ML before PYTHON3 from the kit's manifest, EXAKIT_UDF_CONTAINER first - and raises
with the fix when none is installed, before anything is written. `model_dir` is accepted for the earlier
signature; the model comes back through the query, in parts of up to 1 MB when it is bigger - no bucket is written. `class_weight` is None or "balanced",
passed to logistic regression and recorded in the plan; it never changes the holdout split.

**Used in:** `ml-engineer/01_train`

## nb.TrainingPlan [#TrainingPlan]

```python
class nb.TrainingPlan
```

What in-database training will run, prepared from an approved, fresh handoff: the feature view and its columns, the
script that creates the training UDF, the training SQL and its parameters.

| Member          | What it is        |
| --------------- | ----------------- |
| `view`          | `str`             |
| `features`      | `tuple[str, ...]` |
| `create_script` | `str`             |
| `training_sql`  | `str`             |
| `params`        | `dict[str, Any]`  |
| `handoff`       | `dict[str, Any]`  |


# Your own file or table (/data-scientist/development/reference/own-file)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

```python
ds = nb.load_own_file("~/data/transactions.csv", "MY_DATA.TRANSACTIONS",
                      {"entity": "CUSTOMER_ID", "category": "MERCHANT_TYPE", "date": "BOOKED_ON",
                       "label": "DISPUTED", "text": ["MEMO"]})
```

The descriptor is that mapping of role to column, a descriptor mapping (`schema_version`, `id`, `fact_table`,
`roles`), or a descriptor file - YAML or JSON; `data/datasets/<id>/descriptor.yaml` in the kit shows the shape -
whose fact_table then names the table (`table` may be None). Given as a mapping of roles, they become a
schema_version 2 \*\*draft\*\* (version 1, drafted by the user, owned by EXAKIT_DESCRIPTOR_OWNER or the OS user, its
`source` the file) and are written beside the file as `<name>.descriptor.yaml` (when no descriptor is there yet),
so `DATASET = "<the file>"` in a notebook opens it again with that one assignment; approving it (the quickstart's
approve(), or exakit describe \<id> --approve) is what the training and question steps wait for, exploring does not.
The rows travel over pyexasol's import on the open connection: no
host, user or password here, as everywhere in exakit.nb. Column types come from the file; the date role's column
becomes a DATE and a true/false column 0 or 1; a JSON file is an array of records or one record per line, its nested
values kept as JSON text. The table is marked as loaded from the file (its comment holds the file's SHA-256), so
running the cell again loads nothing when the file is unchanged and reloads it when it changed; a table of the same
name that this did not create is refused unless `replace=True`.

## nb.load_own_file [#load_own_file]

```python
nb.load_own_file(
    path: str | Path,
    table: str | None,
    descriptor: Any=None,
    *,
    conn=None,
    replace: bool=False,
    missing_ok: bool=False,
) -> Dataset | LoadedTable | None
```

Load your own data and return it as a Dataset the notebooks run on (or a LoadedTable whose roles are reviewed
next). `path` is a CSV, Parquet or JSON file, or a folder of them (loaded by `exakit data-load`, exapump, one
table per file). `table` is the schema the tables go into (empty: the folder's name), each named after its file; or
SCHEMA.TABLE to name the file's table, or the folder's table to describe next.
`descriptor` (a file only) maps each role to a column of the file (`text` may name several), or is a
descriptor mapping or file (YAML or JSON; its fact_table names the table when `table` is None). `conn`
defaults to a new exakit.nb.connect(). With `missing_ok`, a path that is not there says so in one line and
returns None.

## nb.LoadedTable [#LoadedTable]

```python
class nb.LoadedTable
```

A file that has been loaded but has not yet received an approved descriptor.

| Member       | What it is |
| ------------ | ---------- |
| `id`         | `str`      |
| `fact_table` | `str`      |
| `path`       | `Path`     |

## nb.save_descriptor [#save_descriptor]

```python
nb.save_descriptor(
    doc: dict[str, Any],
    path: str | Path,
    about: str='',
    *,
    status: str | None=None,
    source: str | None=None,
) -> Path
```

Write a descriptor document as YAML, in the layout of the kit's own descriptor.yaml files - always as
schema_version 2: a schema_version 1 document (or one without the record keys) is written as version 1 with
`status` (draft unless the document, or `status`, says approved), the owner (EXAKIT_DESCRIPTOR_OWNER, else the
OS user), created now, drafted by the user and, when given, `source` (`file:<path>` for a file's descriptor).
What the document already records is kept as it is.

## nb.use_table [#use_table]

```python
nb.use_table(conn, table: str) -> LoadedTable
```

A table already in the database, to describe next (review_roles): `SCHEMA.TABLE`. A table whose columns kept
their file's names ("Won", "Opportunity ID") cannot be read by unquoted queries, so it gets a view with plain
names over it in the prepared schema, said in one line; the table itself is never changed.


# Typed view (/data-scientist/development/reference/prepare)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

A file loaded as text (every column VARCHAR, as CSVs often are), blank cells, placeholder values and rows copied twice
all make a result quietly wrong. typed_view() reads the table - not just its names - and proposes one view over it:

```python
- a text column whose every value parses as a number becomes DECIMAL (DOUBLE with an exponent), as a date (in one
  of the formats below) DATE, as a timestamp TIMESTAMP, as true/false BOOLEAN; an identifier, and a number written
  with a leading zero, and a column named like a code (postal code, phone, SKU, ..._ID), stay text;
- text is trimmed and a blank cell becomes NULL;
- the placeholders the data checks find ("Unknown Device", "N/A", ...) become NULL;
- rows that are exact copies of another in every column but the key are dropped (the first, by the key, is kept).
```

Nothing is written until `create()`: the proposal shows each change with the evidence for it and the exact SQL. Then
the view goes into the EXAKIT_PREPARED schema, and it gets its own approved descriptor - the same roles as the table it
came from, a column that became a date filling an empty time slot - so every later step reads the prepared data.

```python
prepared = nb.typed_view(conn, ds)     # the proposal: what changes, why, and the CREATE VIEW
ds = prepared.create(conn)             # the view, described and approved; the dataset from here on
```

## nb.typed_view [#typed_view]

```python
nb.typed_view(conn, ds) -> TypedView
```

The proposal for `ds`'s table: its types, its cleaning and the CREATE VIEW, built from the data and the
descriptor. Only SELECTs run; nothing is created until `create()`.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/01_explore`

## nb.TypedView [#TypedView]

```python
class nb.TypedView
```

The proposal. `changes` and `cleaning` say what the view does differently from the table, `sql` is the
CREATE VIEW that `create()` runs - nothing has run before that.

| Member                | What it is                                                                                                                                                            |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `dataset`             | `Any`                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `view`                | `str`                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `sql`                 | `str`                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `changes`             | `list[Change]`                                                                                                                                                        |
| `cleaning`            | `list[str]`                                                                                                                                                           |
| `created`             | `Any`                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `needed`              | Whether the view would differ from the table at all.                                                                                                                  |
| `create(conn) -> Any` | Create the view (after the user has read it), describe it, carry the table's roles over and approve them; returns the view's dataset, which the later steps then use. |


# Providers (/data-scientist/development/reference/providers)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

```python
nb.model_providers()                          # OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral, Groq, Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, other
nb.provider_models("anthropic")               # asks for the key (hidden), returns the models it may use
nb.effort_levels("openai", "o4-mini")         # ["low", "medium", "high"]; [] when the model takes no effort setting
```

Each provider is reached through its OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions address, the one the kit's client speaks
(model_config.py). Listing the models is one GET with the key, to the provider only (never anywhere else, never
over plain http to another computer); the key is not kept here. Effort is the provider's own `reasoning_effort`:
offered only where the provider documents it for that model. Anthropic's OpenAI-compatible API ignores it, so a
Claude model is offered none.

## nb.effort_levels [#effort_levels]

```python
nb.effort_levels(provider_id: str, model_id: str) -> list[str]
```

The effort levels this model takes (sent as reasoning_effort); \[] when the provider documents none for it.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/00_quickstart`

## nb.model_providers [#model_providers]

```python
nb.model_providers() -> list[dict[str, Any]]
```

Every provider the notebooks offer: id, name, the Chat Completions address, whether it needs a key
("required", "optional", "none"), where to get one, and whether it runs on this computer.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/00_quickstart`

## nb.provider_models [#provider_models]

```python
nb.provider_models(
    provider_id: str,
    api_key: str | None=None,
    *,
    base_url: str='',
    headers: dict[str, str] | None=None,
    ask=None,
) -> list[str]
```

The chat models this key may use, sorted, from the provider's own list (one GET to the provider). The key is
asked for in a hidden prompt when the provider needs one and none is given; it is used for this call only.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/00_quickstart`


# Draft SQL without a model (/data-scientist/development/reference/question-rules)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

```python
proposal = nb.draft_question(connection, dataset, "Which category has the highest cancellation rate?")
proposal.approve(); answer = proposal.run()        # the kit's own path, as for a model's draft (nb.ask)
```

It matches common question shapes (rate, count, total, average per group; top N; trend over time; filters by year
and by a group's value) to SQL templates over the approved column map, checks the SQL is read-only, and hands it to
nb.ask(proposed_sql=...), so approval, logging and running are the kit's. `example_questions(dataset)` suggests
questions this dataset's roles can answer. Nothing leaves the computer: no model is called.

## nb.draft_question [#draft_question]

```python
nb.draft_question(conn, ds, question: str)
```

A Proposal for `question` drafted by rules from the column map (no AI model): read-only SQL, with the
drafter's assumptions, not approved yet. Approve and run it as any proposal.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/02_ask_your_data`

## nb.example_questions [#example_questions]


Up to three questions this dataset's approved roles can answer, in its own column names.

# Quickstart steps (/data-scientist/development/reference/quickstart)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

The steps both quickstarts share (notebook/notebooks/00_shared): is the database there, what does it hold, and one
loader per way data comes in - a sample dataset the kit ships, your own file, an external source connected as a
virtual schema. Each loader is one cell's call; one that is not set up says so in one line and returns None, so a
notebook runs top to bottom whichever ways the user picked.

```python
conn = nb.connect()
nb.check_connection(conn); nb.list_schemas(conn)
sample = nb.load_sample(conn, "amazon_sales")
own = nb.load_own_file("~/data/sales.json", "MY_DATA.SALES", {...}, conn=conn, missing_ok=True)
source = nb.load_source(conn, None)
ds = nb.first(source, own, sample); nb.show_roles(ds)
```

Nothing here prints a host, a user or a password.

## nb.check_connection [#check_connection]

```python
nb.check_connection(conn)
```

The database answers: its time, this session's id and its version, as one row (and one line).

## nb.connected_sources [#connected_sources]

```python
nb.connected_sources(conn)
```

The virtual schemas in the database (external sources) with their number of tables; empty when there is none.

## nb.first [#first]

```python
nb.first(*candidates: Dataset | LoadedTable | None) -> Dataset | LoadedTable
```

The first dataset that was loaded, in the order given; says which one is used.

## nb.list_schemas [#list_schemas]

```python
nb.list_schemas(conn)
```

Every schema with its number of tables, virtual ones (connected sources) marked.

## nb.load_sample [#load_sample]

```python
nb.load_sample(conn, dataset_id: str | None) -> Dataset | None
```

A dataset the kit offers (`amazon_sales`, `fraud_transactions`): used as it is when it is loaded, else loaded
first with `exakit data-load <id>` (the cell waits for it), then checked against the database. None skips it.

## nb.load_source [#load_source]

```python
nb.load_source(conn, descriptor: str | Path | None) -> Dataset | LoadedTable | None
```

A table in a connected external source (a virtual schema). `descriptor` is `VS_<NAME>.<TABLE>` (any case,
the VS\_ prefix optional), `VS_<NAME>` alone (its one table, or a list of them), or a descriptor file whose
fact_table is in a source. None skips it and lists the sources there are. A name that cannot be used stops the
cell with one line naming what is there and how to connect one; the table is read once (one row) to prove it.

## nb.show_roles [#show_roles]

```python
nb.show_roles(ds: Dataset) -> None
```

The descriptor's roles, one per line, as the notebook will use them.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/01_explore`, `data-scientist/02_ask_your_data`


# Plain-language notes (/data-scientist/development/reference/readout)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

```python
by = nb.name(CATEGORY)                              # CATEGORY: result columns are named after the data
pct = nb.name(LABEL, "PCT")                         # CANCELLED_PCT: the % of rows where CANCELLED is 1
count = nb.count_name(ds)                           # ORDER_LINES: the count column, named after what a row is
nb.note_groups(first_rows, ds, by, count, pct, overall=(128975, 14.2))
nb.note_trend(over_time, ds, "PERIOD", count, pct)
nb.note_model(auc, ds, rows=20000)
```

Each note says what one row of the result is, what each number means in the data's own words (`ds.grain`: "one
row per order line" makes them order lines), the overall figure, the highest and lowest groups, which groups are too small to
trust, and that a difference between groups is not a cause. Nothing is computed that the result does not hold.

## nb.count_name [#count_name]

```python
nb.count_name(ds) -> str
```

The count column, named after what is counted: ORDER_LINES, STORE_WEEKS; ROW_COUNT when the descriptor does
not say (ROWS is an SQL word).

**Used in:** `data-scientist/00_quickstart`, `data-scientist/01_explore`, `data-scientist/02_ask_your_data`, `data-scientist/03_share`, `ml-engineer/00_quickstart`

## nb.name [#name]

```python
nb.name(column: str | None, suffix: str='') -> str
```

A result column named after a data column: `CANCELLED` + `PCT` -> `CANCELLED_PCT`; quotes, dots and
spaces become underscores, so the name works unquoted in SQL.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/00_quickstart`, `data-scientist/01_explore`, `data-scientist/02_ask_your_data`, `data-scientist/03_share`, `ml-engineer/00_quickstart`

## nb.note_groups [#note_groups]

```python
nb.note_groups(
    frame,
    ds,
    by: str | tuple[str, ...],
    rows: str='ROW_COUNT',
    pct: str | None=None,
    *,
    overall: tuple[Any, Any] | None=None,
) -> str
```

Print (and return) the note under a per-group result: one line per fact, in the data's own words.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/00_quickstart`, `data-scientist/01_explore`, `ml-engineer/00_quickstart`

## nb.note_model [#note_model]

```python
nb.note_model(auc: float, ds, rows: int, share: float | None=None) -> str
```

Print (and return) the note under the small model's score, in words.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/01_explore`

## nb.note_trend [#note_trend]

```python
nb.note_trend(frame, ds, period: str='PERIOD', rows: str='ROW_COUNT', pct: str | None=None) -> str
```

Print (and return) the note under a per-period result: the busiest period and the highest and lowest %.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/01_explore`

## nb.noun [#noun]

```python
nb.noun(ds, one: bool=False) -> str
```

What a row is, from the descriptor's grain: "one row per order line" -> "order lines" (`one=True`: "order
line"), "one row per store and week" -> "store weeks"; at most three words, up to a comma or a word such as "in" or
"per"; "rows" when the descriptor does not say.


# Review and approve roles (/data-scientist/development/reference/role-picker)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

```python
review = nb.review_roles(conn, ds)        # profiles the table, prints the evidence, shows the picker
ds = review.dataset()                     # the approved dataset; waits for the approval
```

The picker is the descriptor itself: one dropdown per column with the eight roles (key, time, measure, category, flag,
text, identifier, other), set to the role the rules drafted and labelled with the evidence that chose it; then one
dropdown per slot - the columns the notebooks use (key, time, text, target, category, entity) - set to the drafted
column; then an Approve button. In JupyterLab it is
ipywidgets; in Marimo the review itself is a `mo.ui.dictionary` of `mo.ui.dropdown` with a `mo.ui.run_button`, so
`ds = review.dataset()` runs again when the button is clicked and stops cleanly (`mo.stop`) until then; in a plain
Python session `review.approve({"COLUMN": "role", ...})` is the same path.

Headless (`EXAKIT_NB_AUTO_APPROVE`, set by `tools/notebooks.py --run`): `1` approves the proposal only when its
roles equal the current approved version's (the kit's store, else the shipped descriptor) - then nothing is written,
no new version, no column comments, so a CI run is idempotent; a proposal that differs stays a draft, the run says
why, and `dataset()` hands the draft on so a step that needs an approval (`require_approved`) says what to do.
`force` approves whatever was proposed: a deliberately scripted approval.

`review_roles(conn, name)` with a notebook's one assignment (a dataset id, a descriptor file, a data file) opens it as
it is described; a data file with no descriptor beside it is loaded, profiled and reviewed right there, the draft
saved beside it so the assignment reopens it. The active workflow's log gets `describe.draft` and
`describe.approve` lines (X-1).

## nb.review_roles [#review_roles]

```python
nb.review_roles(conn, source: Any) -> RoleReview
```

Profile the loaded sample, file or connected table, show evidence and role choices, then await approval. Given
a name (a notebook's one assignment: a dataset id, a descriptor file, a data file with its roles beside it) the
dataset is opened as it is described and nothing is profiled; a data file with no descriptor beside it is loaded
and reviewed here.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/01_explore`

## nb.RoleReview [#RoleReview]

```python
class nb.RoleReview
```

One proposal. Jupyter shows a dropdown per column and an Approve button; elsewhere approve(choices) is the same
path. dataset() stops the next cell until approval happened (a headless run hands the draft on, see the module).

| Member                                                                                                          | What it is                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `suggestions() -> dict[str, str]`                                                                               | \{column: drafted role} (one of the eight), in table order.                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `low_confidence() -> list[str]`                                                                                 | The columns drafted at low confidence, in table order: where the draft guessed, so a person looks first.                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `review_order() -> list[str]`                                                                                   | The columns as the pickers show them: low confidence first, then the rest, each in table order.                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `slot_suggestions() -> dict[str, str \| None]`                                                                  | \{slot: drafted column or None}: the columns the notebooks use.                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `labels() -> dict[str, tuple[str, str]]`                                                                        | \{column: (summary, note)}: the column's type, role and confidence with the evidence that chose the role, and its model note when there is one.                                                                                                                                   |
| `guide() -> str`                                                                                                | Explain what is measured and what the user must decide, in every front end.                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `explanations() -> dict[str, str]`                                                                              | Plain reasons beside the evidence; a low-confidence role says so, and certainty is never implied.                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `approve( choices: dict[str, str \| None] \| None=None, slots: dict[str, str \| None] \| None=None) -> Dataset` | Apply the reviewed roles (\{COLUMN: role}, one of the eight; the proposal when None) and slots (\{slot: COLUMN or None}), then save and comment the approved descriptor.                                                                                                          |
| `auto_approve(mode: str) -> str`                                                                                | The headless decision for EXAKIT_NB_AUTO_APPROVE=`mode`: `force` approves the proposal; `1` approves only a proposal whose roles equal the current approved version's - then nothing is written (`unchanged`); a proposal that differs stays a `draft` and the reason is printed. |
| `dataset(draft_ok: bool=False) -> Dataset`                                                                      | The approved dataset: the one approved here, else the approved version the review opened on.                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `show()`                                                                                                        | Print the proposal with its evidence, then the picker the front end has (or the headless decision).                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `jupyter_picker()`                                                                                              | The ipywidgets picker, or None when this is not a Jupyter kernel with ipywidgets.                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `build_jupyter_picker(widgets)`                                                                                 | One dropdown per column with the eight roles (the drafted one set), its reason and evidence under it - the columns drafted at low confidence first, under their own heading; then one dropdown per slot with the table's columns; then the Approve button.                        |


# Schema map and joined view (/data-scientist/development/reference/schema-map)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

A table's column map says what its columns are; the schema map says how the schema's tables fit together - every
table with its rows and key, and every many-to-one link between them, declared by the database or found (a column
that names another table's key and whose every value is in it), each with its evidence. The kit's describe service
does the work (setup/lib/descriptor/schema.py); this module shows it in a notebook and turns it into a dataset:

```python
schema_map = nb.describe_schema(connection, dataset)        # the tables and the links, as found now
joined = schema_map.joined_view(dataset)                    # the main table with every table its links reach
dataset = joined.create(connection)                         # approves the map, creates the view, its column map
```

Nothing is written before create(): the proposal shows every join and the exact SQL. Then the schema map is approved
(its links become relationships of the schema's Exasol Semantic Views model, for agents), the view goes into EXAKIT_PREPARED and gets
its own approved column map - the main table's roles carried over - so every later step reads the joined data.

## nb.describe_schema [#describe_schema]

```python
nb.describe_schema(connection, dataset_or_schema: Any) -> SchemaMap
```

The schema of `dataset_or_schema` (a dataset, or a schema name) as found now: its tables, rows and keys, and
every many-to-one link between them with its evidence. A live source's schema is not surveyed (its tables are
queried in place, every count a round trip).

**Used in:** `data-scientist/01_explore`

## nb.JoinedView [#JoinedView]

```python
class nb.JoinedView
```

The proposal for one wide view. `joins` lists each table it adds and how; `sql` is what create() runs.

| Member                      | What it is                                                                                                                                                       |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `schema_map`                | `SchemaMap`                                                                                                                                                      |
| `view`                      | \`str                                                                                                                                                            | None\` |
| `main`                      | `str`                                                                                                                                                            |
| `built`                     | `dict[str, Any]`                                                                                                                                                 |
| `source_id`                 | \`str                                                                                                                                                            | None\` |
| `source`                    | `Any`                                                                                                                                                            |
| `created`                   | `Any`                                                                                                                                                            |
| `joins`                     |                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `needed`                    | Whether the main table has links to follow at all.                                                                                                               |
| `sql`                       |                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `create(connection) -> Any` | Approve the schema map (when it is a draft), create the view, describe it with the main table's roles carried over and approve that; returns the view's dataset. |

## nb.SchemaMap [#SchemaMap]

```python
class nb.SchemaMap
```

The schema as found (a draft) or as approved: `doc` holds its tables and links.

| Member                                        | What it is                                                                                            |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `doc`                                         | \`dict\[str, Any]                                                                                     | None\` |
| `approved_version`                            | \`int                                                                                                 | None\` |
| `note`                                        | \`str                                                                                                 | None\` |
| `schema`                                      |                                                                                                       |
| `links`                                       |                                                                                                       |
| `link(source: str, target: str) -> SchemaMap` | Add a link the search missed: `link("ORDERS.CUSTOMER_REF", "CUSTOMERS.ID")`.                          |
| `unlink(source: str) -> SchemaMap`            | Remove a link that is wrong, by the column it starts from: `unlink("ORDERS.O_CLERK")`.                |
| `approve(connection) -> SchemaMap`            | Approve this map (the next version in the store; the schema's semantic model rebuilt with its links). |
| `joined_view(main: Any) -> JoinedView`        | The proposal: `main` (a dataset, or a table name) with every table its links reach.                   |


# Semantic (/data-scientist/development/reference/semantic)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

```python
model = nb.semantic_model(connection, "sales_360",
                          tables=["AMAZON_SALES.ORDER_LINES", "MY_DATA.TARGETS", "VS_LOGISTICS.COURIER_DAILY"],
                          links=["AMAZON_SALES.ORDER_LINES.STATE=VS_LOGISTICS.STATE_LOGISTICS.STATE"],
                          preview=True)            # what it would build, and what the AI proposes; nothing written
model = model.publish()                             # build it in the database (Semantic Views installed if needed)
nb.find_links(connection, ["AMAZON", "VS_LOGISTICS", "MY_DATA"])     # links across sources, from the values
nb.semantic_model(connection, "all_data", schemas=["AMAZON", "VS_LOGISTICS", "MY_DATA"], find=True)
nb.semantic_models(connection)                      # every model in the database
nb.refresh_semantic(connection, "sales_360")        # rebuild it after a column map or a link changed
nb.semantic_sql(connection, "SELECT order_month, total_revenue FROM SEM_SALES_360.ORDER_LINES GROUP BY order_month")
```

A model spans as many schemas as you give it: sample datasets, your own loaded files and folders, and any number of
connected external sources (virtual schemas, read live). Every table needs an approved column map first: its roles
decide the model's fields - time, category and flag columns become dimensions, measures become facts with total\_ and
average\_ metrics, every table gets a row count. The approved links of each schema are used, and `links` adds the
ones across schemas (SCHEMA.TABLE.COLUMN=SCHEMA.TABLE.KEY, the key side unique).

With `ai=True` (the default when a model is configured: nb.model_setup) your model proposes business names,
comments and synonyms for every field and the metrics people will ask for - from names, types, grains, column notes
and a category's top values only, never a row and never a sensitive column. Every proposed metric is checked before
it is offered, and the product validates it again when it is applied: a refused one is skipped and named.

The work is the kit's describe service (the one `exakit describe --model` runs), loaded from the kit copy. A model
the kit builds is marked as such; one of the same name somebody else made is never touched.

## nb.find_links [#find_links]

```python
nb.find_links(
    conn,
    schemas: list[str],
    *,
    ai: bool | None=None,
    check: list[str] | None=None,
    show: bool=True,
) -> dict[str, Any]
```

The links between tables of different schemas - sample data, your files, external sources - where no foreign
key says so and the names differ, found from the values, each with its evidence (`exakit describe --links`).
Bounded reads only; nothing is written. `ai` (default: when a model is configured) lets your model propose more
pairs from names, types and notes; `check` is pairs you have in mind ("S.T.COL=S.T.KEY"); each is checked against
the data and comes back with its evidence or under "rejected". Returns \{links, partial, ...}; a link's
`confidence` is "low" for plain numbers, which match by chance: confirm those before using them.

## nb.refresh_semantic [#refresh_semantic]

```python
nb.refresh_semantic(conn, name: str) -> dict[str, Any]
```

Rebuild a model the kit published, with the column maps and links approved since (`exakit describe --model
NAME --refresh`). Approving a column map refreshes every model it is in by itself.

## nb.semantic_model [#semantic_model]

```python
nb.semantic_model(
    conn,
    name: str,
    tables: list[str] | None=None,
    links: list[str] | None=None,
    *,
    schemas: list[str] | None=None,
    find: bool=False,
    ai: bool | None=None,
    description: str | None=None,
    preview: bool=False,
) -> SemanticModel
```

Build (or with `preview=True` only show) an Exasol Semantic Views model over `tables` - SCHEMA.TABLE of any
schemas, each with an approved column map - joined along each schema's approved links and `links`
(SCHEMA.TABLE.COLUMN=SCHEMA.TABLE.KEY). `schemas` takes every table of those schemas that has an approved column
map; `find=True` finds the links between the schemas from their values (nb.find_links) and uses the ones the
data backs. `ai` (default: when a model is configured) lets your model propose the
fields' business names, synonyms and extra metrics. Publishing installs Semantic Views when the database does not
have it, replaces the model the kit built before under that name, and grants it to the read-only MCP user.

## nb.semantic_models [#semantic_models]

```python
nb.semantic_models(conn)
```

Every semantic model in the database: name, published schema, whether the kit built it (and can refresh it).

## nb.semantic_sql [#semantic_sql]

```python
nb.semantic_sql(conn, query: str)
```

Run Semantic SQL (a query over a published semantic view: its metrics with GROUP BY its dimensions) on this
connection: Semantic SQL is switched on for the session first. A read only, shown before its result.

## nb.SemanticModel [#SemanticModel]

```python
class nb.SemanticModel
```

A semantic model: what it holds (`spec`), what the AI proposed, and - once published - its views.

| Member                                | What it is                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`                                | `str`                                                                                               |
| `tables`                              | `list[str]`                                                                                         |
| `links`                               | `list[str]`                                                                                         |
| `description`                         | \`str                                                                                               | None\` |
| `ai`                                  | `bool`                                                                                              |
| `found`                               | `dict[str, Any]`                                                                                    |
| `conn`                                | `Any`                                                                                               |
| `schemas`                             | `list[str]`                                                                                         |
| `find`                                | `bool`                                                                                              |
| `status`                              |                                                                                                     |
| `views`                               |                                                                                                     |
| `spec`                                |                                                                                                     |
| `fields`                              | One row per dimension and metric: view, kind, name, display name, what it is.                       |
| `publish(conn=None) -> SemanticModel` | Build the previewed model in the database (the AI's proposal is asked again only if none was kept). |


# Model, Langfuse and MLflow settings (/data-scientist/development/reference/setup-env)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

They are the environment variables `exakit notebook` already reads (EXAKIT_MODEL_ID, EXAKIT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL,
EXAKIT_PROVIDER_API_KEY, LANGFUSE\_\*, MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI), so a cell is one more way to give them, not another kind of
setting. The plain values come from the cell. The keys are asked for in a hidden prompt and kept in this kernel's
environment only: never in the notebook or its outputs, and gone when the kernel stops - unless `remember=True`,
which saves them beside the kit's credentials (readable by this user only, 0600) so every notebook's kernel has them
(`import exakit.nb` loads them; `forget_model()` deletes them). A key already set (by
the shell that started JupyterLab, or an earlier run of the cell) is not asked again - unless the address it was for
changed. Empty values change nothing, so a cell left as shipped is a no-op and a headless run never waits on a prompt.

## nb.forget_model [#forget_model]

```python
nb.forget_model(model: bool=True, langfuse: bool=True) -> None
```

Delete what use_model(..., remember=True) saved (the model, Langfuse, or both) and clear it from this kernel.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/00_quickstart`

## nb.model_setup [#model_setup]

```python
nb.model_setup(
    machine: str | None=None,
    show: bool=True,
    *,
    ask: bool | None=None,
    read: Ask | None=None,
    secret: Ask | None=None,
) -> dict
```

Set up your model and Langfuse for this kernel, and say how to set them for every notebook. Inside a notebook
(JupyterLab or Marimo) it first asks for what is missing - the model id and address, the Langfuse address, then
each key in a hidden box; Enter skips one. `ask=False` only reports; a script or test never waits on a prompt.
Then it prints what is set and, for anything still missing, the terminal lines for this machine (Windows, Mac,
Linux or WSL). Prints values, never a key; returns \{"machine", "set", "missing", "lines", "asked"}.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/01_explore`, `data-scientist/02_ask_your_data`

## nb.use_mlflow [#use_mlflow]

```python
nb.use_mlflow(tracking_uri: str='', login: bool=False, *, ask: Ask | None=None) -> dict
```

The MLflow server this kernel records runs to: `tracking_uri` (empty: the kit's own MLflow, or what the shell
set); `login=True` asks for the server's username and password (hidden). Prints where runs go, never a password.

**Used in:** `ml-engineer/00_quickstart`, `ml-engineer/01_train`

## nb.use_model [#use_model]

```python
nb.use_model(
    model_id: str='',
    provider_base_url: str='',
    langfuse_base_url: str='',
    *,
    effort: str | None=None,
    ask: Ask | None=None,
    remember: bool=False,
) -> dict
```

Your model and Langfuse tracing for this kernel. `model_id` and `provider_base_url` (a Chat Completions base
URL) set the model and ask for its API key (Enter for none: a local server); `effort` sets how hard a reasoning
model thinks ("low", "medium", "high"; "" for the model's default; nb.effort_levels says which a model takes);
`langfuse_base_url` turns tracing on and asks for its two keys. Prints what is in use, never a key; returns that summary.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/00_quickstart`, `data-scientist/01_explore`, `data-scientist/02_ask_your_data`


# Share a dashboard (/data-scientist/development/reference/share)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

`tool` is a callable for the registered dash-server MCP tools. Notebook cells
use the kit-managed MCP endpoint through `dash_tools()`.
The dashboard itself queries Exasol through Dash Server's server-side profile.

## nb.share [#share]

```python
nb.share(dataset: Any, sql: str, title: str, name: str, *, measure: str='value') -> ShareDraft
```

Make a draft from approved data and inspected SQL; measure=count enables count totals and composition.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/03_share`

## nb.ShareDraft [#ShareDraft]

```python
class nb.ShareDraft
```

A dashboard prepared from an approved dataset and one query. `preview()` puts it on Dash Server as a preview;
`confirm(..., figures_checked=True)` publishes it, and only after a person checked the preview's figures.

| Member                                                                                    | What it is                                                                 |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `dataset`                                                                                 | `Any`                                                                      |
| `sql`                                                                                     | `str`                                                                      |
| `title`                                                                                   | `str`                                                                      |
| `name`                                                                                    | `str`                                                                      |
| `query_digest`                                                                            | `str`                                                                      |
| `workflow_id`                                                                             | `str`                                                                      |
| `files`                                                                                   | `list[dict[str, str]]`                                                     |
| `revision_number`                                                                         | \`int                                                                      | None\` |
| `preview_url`                                                                             | \`str                                                                      | None\` |
| `healthy`                                                                                 | `bool`                                                                     |
| `requests(profile_name: str='starter-kit') -> list[tuple[str, dict[str, Any]]]`           | The exact MCP calls an agent makes to create the preview (no credentials). |
| `description() -> str`                                                                    | The catalog's line under the title: the approved data it answers from.     |
| `preview(tool: Tool, profile_name: str='starter-kit', windows: bool \| None=None) -> str` | Create and health-check a preview; on Windows use build + healthcheck.     |
| `confirm(tool: Tool, figures_checked: bool=False) -> str`                                 | Promote the exact healthy preview after a human checks its figures.        |


# External sources (/data-scientist/development/reference/sources)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

```python
nb.connect_source("postgresql", "sales", url="postgres://reader@192.168.64.1:5432/shop")   # asks the password
nb.connect_source("postgresql", "sales", host="192.168.64.1", database="shop", user="reader")
nb.clean_path("'/Users/me/My Data/orders.csv'")    # a pasted path: quotes, file://, "\ " and ~ undone
```

connect_source runs `exakit connect <connector> --name <name> ... --password-stdin --yes --json`. The password is
asked in a hidden box and goes to the command on standard input: never into the cell, the command line or a log.

## nb.clean_path [#clean_path]

```python
nb.clean_path(value: Any) -> str
```

A path pasted into a cell, made usable: quotes and spaces around it, a `file://` link, the shell's
backslash escapes (`My\ Data`, from a drag into a terminal) and `~` are undone. Empty stays empty.

## nb.connect_source [#connect_source]

```python
nb.connect_source(
    connector: str,
    name: str,
    url: str | None=None,
    *,
    password: Any=None,
    password_file: str | Path | None=None,
    ask_password: bool=True,
    dry_run: bool=False,
    show: bool=True,
    secret: Callable[[str], str] | None=None,
    storage_secret: Any=None,
    storage_secret_file: str | Path | None=None,
    **settings: Any,
) -> str | None
```

Connect an external source as a virtual schema, from a notebook cell. `connector` is the kit's id or alias
(`postgresql`, `pg`, `mysql`, `snowflake` ...; `exakit help connect` lists them), `name` becomes the
schema `VS_<NAME>`. Give the source's connection string as `url` (a JDBC URL, `postgres://...`), or each
input as a keyword (`host=`, `database=`, `schema=`, `user=` ...; the connector's skill lists them).
The password is asked in a hidden box (Enter: none), or read from `password_file`; a password inside `url` is
taken out of it and used, never shown. Marimo has no hidden prompt: pass a password field as `password`
(`mo.ui.text(kind="password")`, its value is read) or a `password_file`. `dry_run` checks the inputs and
connects nothing. A connector with several kinds of source in one takes its settings as keywords too
(`catalog="unity", files="s3"` for a Lakehouse; nb.connector_inputs lists them). A source with a second secret
(a Lakehouse catalog login plus storage keys) takes it as `storage_secret_file`, or as `storage_secret` (the
text, a Marimo password field, or a function that asks for it): it reaches the kit in a file only this user can
read, removed as soon as the kit has read it. Returns the schema name (`VS_SALES`) when connected, None for a dry run; raises SourceProblem with the kit's reason otherwise.

## nb.read_connection_string [#read_connection_string]

```python
nb.read_connection_string(connector: str, text: str, **settings: Any) -> dict[str, Any]
```

Read a source's connection string exactly as `exakit connect --url` does: it is handed to the kit's engine
(its `paste` command, on standard input, never as an argument). Returns \{connector, values, notes, dropped,
masked, credential_in_string, secret_input, missing}: `values` by input name, each checked as if typed;
`masked` the string with every credential as \*\*\*\*; `missing` the connector's required inputs the string does
not give (and no default covers). The string's password is used by nb.connect_source(url=...) and is never
returned, printed or logged here. For a connector with settings (a Lakehouse's `catalog=`, `files=`) give the
ones already chosen: a setting the string itself shows (an s3:// path
is a folder with no catalog) comes back in `values`, and `missing` is what that combination still needs.

## nb.source_engine [#source_engine]

```python
nb.source_engine(*words: str, text: str | None=None) -> dict[str, Any]
```

Ask the kit's own source engine (setup/virtual-schemas/engine/cli.py, the coordinator behind `exakit connect`
and `exakit source`) one of the questions its connect form asks, and return its --json answer:

```python
source_engine("catalog")                      the connectors, as the connect menu lists them
source_engine("inputs", "postgresql")         what the form asks for one, in order
source_engine("field", "postgresql", "port", text="5433")    is this answer right? (the value on stdin)
source_engine("paste", "postgresql", text=...)               a connection string, read into inputs
```

Run as the kit's shell runs it: the kit's Python where it is installed, isolated (-I), with this installation's
definitions and home. None of these four touches the database. A refusal is a SourceProblem in the engine's
words, with its remedy.

## nb.SourceProblem [#SourceProblem]

```python
exception nb.SourceProblem
```

A source cell that cannot go on, said in one short message: no traceback in a notebook.

## nb.SourceTest [#SourceTest]

```python
class nb.SourceTest
```

What test_source found, one check per line: (what was checked, passed, what it said).

| Member      | What it is                    |
| ----------- | ----------------------------- |
| `connector` | `str`                         |
| `name`      | `str`                         |
| `checks`    | `list[tuple[str, bool, str]]` |
| `ok`        |                               |

## nb.test_source [#test_source]

```python
nb.test_source(
    connector: str,
    name: str,
    url: str | None=None,
    *,
    password_file: str | Path | None=None,
    timeout: float=5,
    **settings: Any,
) -> SourceTest
```

Test a source before connecting it, changing nothing: first the kit's own check of every input
(`exakit connect ... --dry-run`), then whether this computer reaches the source's host and port. No password is
needed or sent. The sign-in itself is checked by nb.connect_source, from the database (exakit source check).


# Themes in text (AI) (/data-scientist/development/reference/themes)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

```python
sample = nb.sql(conn, SAMPLE_SQL)                   # LABEL_ and TEXT_: the newest texts on each side of the label
themes = nb.themes(conn, ds, sample, nb.model_client(), sql=SAMPLE_SQL)
```

One model call per side (label = 1, label = 0): the model sorts that side's texts into two to four themes
and answers in JSON, so the result is a table - theme, how many texts, their share, an example - with a note in plain
words under it. A theme found on one side only is the clue: what those texts are about that the others are not.

With Langfuse set up (nb.trace), both calls are one trace, `explore-themes`, each call named after its side, with
what was sent, the answer, tokens, cost and time, and two scores to compare models and runs by: `valid_json` (1 when
every answer could be read) and `texts_placed` (the share of texts the model gave a theme).

## nb.themes [#themes]

```python
nb.themes(conn, ds, sample, endpoint, *, sql: str | None=None)
```

Sort each side's texts into themes with `endpoint` = (client, model) from nb.model_client(); return the table
(a pandas DataFrame when pandas is there, else a list of rows) and print the note. None without an endpoint.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/01_explore`


# Workflows (/data-scientist/development/reference/workflow)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from the docstrings in notebook/package/exakit_nb. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

One workflow id on everything (X-1): `workflow()` starts or resumes one, and every helper that does something
appends a line to its log while it is active - a statement, a trace, an MLflow run, a descriptor draft or approval, a
handoff, a dashboard revision, a model put. Without a workflow nothing is written: there are no implicit workflows.

```python
import exakit.nb as nb
wf = nb.workflow("churn-baseline")        # Workflow wf-20261027-3f9a1c: log ~/.exasol-starter-kit/workflows/...
nb.workflow(resume="wf-20261027-3f9a1c")  # later, in another kernel
nb.continue_workflow("explore")           # the one already going: this kernel's, inherited, or the last one started
```

A notebook never needs an id pasted in: the quickstart starts the work and every later notebook continues it with
`continue_workflow`, which takes this kernel's workflow, else the one inherited through EXAKIT_WORKFLOW_ID, else the
last one started or resumed on this machine ($EXAKIT_HOME/last-workflow), and starts a new one only when there is none.

The id is `wf-YYYYMMDD-<6 hex>`, kept in the session store and in EXAKIT_WORKFLOW_ID so a child process (a CLI call
from a notebook) inherits it. The log is `$EXAKIT_HOME/workflows/<id>.jsonl` (EXAKIT_HOME default
\~/.exasol-starter-kit), append-only, one JSON object per line: `{ts, workflow_id, kind, ...payload}`; the folder is
0700 and the file 0600, each line one O_APPEND write so two kernels on one workflow never interleave. A log that
cannot be written warns and the cell goes on: logging never fails the work it describes.

Credential-shaped payload keys are checked recursively, including JSON-encoded metadata strings. A secret-named key
or a DSN containing a password is refused (a
ValueError - the caller's mistake, before anything is written). SQL text is screened rather than refused: a statement
that mentions PASSWORD, API_KEY, IDENTIFIED BY and the like - or carries a DSN with a password - is logged with its
text replaced by `<redacted: credential-like SQL>` and `redacted: true`, its digest kept, and one warning; the
logger never fails the query it records, which has already run. Other SQL text is kept so the user can find the
query again.

`python -m exakit_nb.workflow list|show <id> [--json]` is what `exakit workflow` runs.

## nb.continue_workflow [#continue_workflow]

```python
nb.continue_workflow(name: str | None=None) -> str
```

The workflow already going, without an id to paste: this kernel's, else the one inherited through
EXAKIT_WORKFLOW_ID, else the last one started or resumed on this machine (a quickstart starts one); a new one named
`name` only when there is none. Says which, and returns the id. The first time a notebook continues a
workflow the log gets one `step` line with `name`, so the kit can tell which notebooks took part.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/01_explore`, `data-scientist/02_ask_your_data`, `data-scientist/03_share`, `ml-engineer/01_train`, `ml-engineer/02_rust_score`

## nb.current_workflow [#current_workflow]

```python
nb.current_workflow() -> str | None
```

The active workflow id: the session's, else the one inherited through EXAKIT_WORKFLOW_ID, else None.

**Used in:** `ml-engineer/02_rust_score`

## nb.last_workflow [#last_workflow]

```python
nb.last_workflow() -> str | None
```

The workflow started or resumed last on this machine, when its log is still there; else None.

## nb.list_workflows [#list_workflows]

```python
nb.list_workflows() -> list[dict]
```

One summary per log in the workflows folder, oldest first: id, name (from its start line), started, last
(first and last timestamps) and events (the line count). An unreadable log is skipped.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/00_quickstart`

## nb.log_event [#log_event]

```python
nb.log_event(kind: str, **payload: Any) -> None
```

Append one line to the active workflow's log; nothing when no workflow is active. A credential-named payload
key or a DSN with a password is a ValueError (the caller's mistake); credential-like statement text is logged
redacted with a warning (never an exception: the statement already ran); a log that cannot be written is a warning
(the environment's).

**Used in:** `ml-engineer/02_rust_score`

## nb.log_sql [#log_sql]

```python
nb.log_sql(conn, statement: str, rows: int | None, statement_id: str | None=None) -> None
```

Log a statement sql() ran: the session and statement ids that find it in the database's audit log, the
statement's SHA-256 (what traces and runs carry), how many rows came back, and the statement text - redacted, with
a warning, when it looks credential-bearing (a PASSWORD or API_KEY column, say); this never raises, the query has
already run. No-op without a workflow; the statement id is looked up on the connection unless given.

**Used in:** `ml-engineer/01_train`

## nb.workflow [#workflow]

```python
nb.workflow(name: str | None=None, resume: str | None=None) -> str
```

Start a workflow (a new id, a `start` line in its log) or, with `resume`, continue an existing one. The id
becomes the session's and EXAKIT_WORKFLOW_ID's, and is returned. Resuming an id whose log does not exist is a
ValueError naming the path, so a typo never starts an empty log under a made-up id.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/00_quickstart`, `ml-engineer/00_quickstart`

## nb.workflow_log [#workflow_log]

```python
nb.workflow_log(workflow_id: str) -> list[dict]
```

Every line of a workflow's log, in order. A missing log is a FileNotFoundError naming the path.

**Used in:** `data-scientist/00_quickstart`
